question: A data engineer needs to ingest from both streaming and batch sources for a firm that relies on highly accurate data. Occasionally, some of the data picked up by the sensors that provide a streaming input are outside the expected parameters. If this occurs, the data must be dropped, but the stream should not fail. Which feature of Delta Live Tables meets this requirement?
optionA: Error Handling
optionB: Change Data Capture
optionC: Monitoring
optionD: Expectations
explanation:
Expectations are the Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines (formerly Delta Live Tables) feature for data quality. An expectation is a constraint plus an action taken when a record violates it, and the documented actions are: warn (EXPECT, the default) writes invalid records to the target; drop (EXPECT ... ON VIOLATION DROP ROW) removes them before the write and logs the dropped count alongside other dataset metrics; fail (EXPECT ... ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE) stops the update entirely. This question asks for the sensor readings outside expected parameters to be dropped while the stream keeps running, which is exactly ON VIOLATION DROP ROW.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Error Handling) — not a named Delta Live Tables feature; there is no "error handling" clause that filters records.
Option B (Change Data Capture) — propagates row changes into a target and does nothing about validity.
Option C (Monitoring) — reports on a pipeline after the fact rather than filtering records inside it.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectations

corrected.note: The documentation names expectations as the data-quality mechanism and lists DROP ROW as the action that discards violating records without failing the update. The two scraped snapshots of this item disagreed: the v2026-06-09 copy keys Expectations and the v2026-07-28 copy keyed Error Handling. The documentation settles it for Expectations.

question: Which of the following describes a scenario in which a data team will want to utilize cluster pools?
optionA: An automated report needs to be refreshed as quickly as possible.
optionB: An automated report needs to be made reproducible.
optionC: An automated report needs to be tested to identify errors.
optionD: An automated report needs to be version-controlled across multiple collaborators.
optionE: An automated report needs to be runnable by all stakeholders.
explanation:
An automated report that needs to be refreshed as quickly as possible is the scenario for cluster pools. A pool is a set of idle, ready-to-use instances, so a cluster attached to it starts and scales without waiting for cloud instances to be provisioned — which is exactly the start-up latency a fast-refresh report is trying to remove. Pools can also save cost by reusing idle instances across clusters, and Databricks does not charge DBUs for instances idling in the pool.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (made reproducible) — reproducibility comes from version control and pinned runtimes, not from pre-warmed instances.
Option C (tested to identify errors) — testing is a matter of the code and its test harness; a pool changes nothing about correctness.
Option D (version-controlled across collaborators) — that is Git integration, not compute configuration.
Option E (runnable by all stakeholders) — access is governed by workspace and job permissions, not by where the cluster's instances come from.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/pool-index

question: A data engineer works for an organization that must meet a stringent Service Level Agreement (SLA) that demands minimal runtime errors and high availability for its data processing pipelines. The data engineer wants to avoid the operational overhead of managing and tuning clusters. Which architectural solution will meet the requirements?
optionA: Deploy a dedicated, manually managed cluster optimized by in-house IT staff.
optionB: Utilize Databricks serverless compute that automatically optimizes resources and abstracts cluster management.
optionC: Use an auto-scaling cluster configured and monitored by the user.
optionD: Implement a hybrid approach with scheduled batch jobs on custom cloud VMs.
explanation:
Databricks serverless compute is the option that removes cluster management entirely. Databricks provisions the capacity, sizes and scales it, applies runtime upgrades and replaces unhealthy instances, so the team gets high availability and consistent performance without anyone tuning a cluster — which is the operational overhead the question wants to avoid.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (dedicated, manually managed cluster) — puts sizing, patching and tuning back on in-house staff, the burden the question is shedding.
Option C (auto-scaling cluster configured and monitored by the user) — still has to be configured and monitored; autoscaling only varies the worker count within bounds someone chose.
Option D (scheduled batch jobs on custom cloud VMs) — abandons the platform's management entirely, the most operational overhead of the four, not the least.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/serverless/

question: Calculate the total sales amount for each region and store the results in a new dataframe called region_sales. Given the expected result: Which code will generate the expected result?
optionA: region sales - sales_df.agg(sum("sales_amount").groupBy("region").alias("total sales amount"))
optionB: region_sales = sales_df.groupBy("region").agg(sum("sales_amountM).alias("total_sales_amount"))
optionC: region_sales= sales_df.groupBy("category").sum(nsales_amount").alias("t_otal_sales_amounl")
optionD: region_sales = sales_df. sum ("salen_aiTiount") . groupBy ("region") .alias ("total_sale3_amount")
explanation:
region_sales = sales_df.groupBy("region").agg(sum("sales_amount").alias("total_sales_amount")) is the pattern for any Spark aggregation: group, then aggregate. It produces one row per region carrying the summed sales amount under the requested column name. As with its sibling question, the printed options carry scrape damage — judge them on structure.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (.agg(sum(...).groupBy("region"))) — nests .groupBy() inside .agg(), which is not valid; grouping must come before aggregation.
Option C (.groupBy("category").sum(...)) — groups by category, answering a different question than the per-region totals asked for.
Option D (.sum(...).groupBy("region")) — calls .sum() before .groupBy(), collapsing the whole DataFrame first and leaving nothing to group.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-groupby

question: What is the maximum output supported by a job cluster to ensure a notebook does not fail?
optionA: 30MBS
optionB: 25MBS
optionC: 15MBS
optionD: 10MBS
explanation:
30 MB is the documented job cluster notebook output ceiling: "Job clusters have a maximum notebook output size of 30 MB." Exceeding it is what fails the notebook, which is what this question asks about.
The 10 MB figure is a different limit and is a default rather than a ceiling: "The maximum cell output size defaults to 10 MB", adjustable per notebook between 1 MB and 20 MB with the %set_cell_max_output_size_in_mb magic, or up to 20 MB on Databricks Runtime 12.2 and above via spark.databricks.driver.maxReplOutputLength. So 10 MB is a per-cell default, 20 MB is the per-cell maximum, and 30 MB is the job cluster output maximum.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (25 MB) — no documented limit; sits between the per-cell maximum and the job cluster ceiling.
Option C (15 MB) — no documented limit.
Option D (10 MB) — the per-cell output default, not the job cluster notebook ceiling, and it can be raised.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/notebooks/notebook-limitations

corrected.note: The Known limitations page states the job cluster maximum notebook output size is 30 MB. The old key of 10 MB was the default maximum cell output size, a per-cell default that is configurable upward -- a default reported as a ceiling.

question: Which of the following benefits is provided by the array functions from Spark SQL?
optionA: An ability to work with data in a variety of types at once
optionB: An ability to work with data within certain partitions and windows
optionC: An ability to work with time-related data in specified intervals
optionD: An ability to work with complex, nested data ingested from JSON files
optionE: An ability to work with an array of tables for procedural automation
explanation:
An ability to work with complex, nested data ingested from JSON files is what Spark SQL's array functions provide. They are the subset of collection functions that operate on array columns: explode turns an array column into one row per element, array_contains tests for a value, array_join concatenates elements with a delimiter, and the higher-order functions (transform, filter, aggregate) apply a lambda to each element. JSON sources routinely arrive with nested arrays and structs, and these functions are how that shape is queried without flattening it first.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a variety of types at once) — a column's array elements share one type; mixed-type handling is not what array functions do.
Option B (data within certain partitions and windows) — that is window functions (OVER ... PARTITION BY), a separate family.
Option C (time-related data in specified intervals) — that is the date and timestamp functions, and window(...) for time buckets.
Option E (an array of tables for procedural automation) — array functions operate on array-typed column values, not on collections of tables.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-functions-builtin

question: A data engineer wants to create a new table containing the names of customers that live in France. They have written the following command: A senior data engineer mentions that it is organization policy to include a table property indicating that the new table includes personally identifiable information (PII). Which of the following lines of code fills in the above blank to successfully complete the task?
optionA: There is no way to indicate whether a table contains PII.
optionB: "COMMENT PII"
optionC: TBLPROPERTIES PII
optionD: COMMENT "Contains PII"
optionE: PII
explanation:
COMMENT "Contains PII" is the line that completes this statement. COMMENT takes a bare string literal in exactly this position, so it parses, and it attaches the PII marker to the table where anyone inspecting it will see it.
TBLPROPERTIES is a genuine way to tag a table, which is what makes it the tempting distractor, but it is not valid on its own. Its documented syntax takes parenthesised key-value pairs — TBLPROPERTIES ( { property_key [ = ] property_val } [, ...] ), where the value must be a BOOLEAN, STRING, INTEGER or DECIMAL literal — so a bare TBLPROPERTIES PII is a syntax error. Written properly it would be TBLPROPERTIES ('PII' = 'true'), which is not what that option offers.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (no way to indicate PII) — false; both COMMENT and TBLPROPERTIES can carry the marker.
Option B ("COMMENT PII") — quotes the keyword itself rather than the message, so it is a string literal where a clause is expected.
Option C (TBLPROPERTIES PII) — a syntax error; TBLPROPERTIES needs parenthesised key-value pairs.
Option E (PII) — a bare word is not a clause at all.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-create-table-using
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-tblproperties

corrected.note: Answer stands. Absorbed the reasoning from the near-duplicate 472fcdb7, which was removed: its option set had been corrupted by the scrape (option A truncated to COMMENT "Contains PIT and option B reduced to 511), so this clean five-option copy is the one worth keeping.

question: Which of the following describes a benefit of creating an external table from Parquet rather than CSV when using a CREATE TABLE AS SELECT statement?
optionA: Parquet files can be partitioned
optionB: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT statements cannot be used on files
optionC: Parquet files have a well-defined schema
optionD: Parquet files have the ability to be optimized
optionE: Parquet files will become Delta tables
explanation:
Parquet files have a well-defined schema, and that is the benefit when creating an external table from them with CREATE TABLE AS SELECT. Column names and types are embedded in the file, so they are detected and preserved automatically. CSV carries no schema, so it has to be declared explicitly or inferred from the data, which costs processing time and invites type and column-name inconsistencies.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Parquet files can be partitioned) — true of both formats; partitioning is a directory layout, not a property of Parquet.
Option B (CTAS cannot be used on files) — false; CREATE TABLE AS SELECT works against a file-backed query such as SELECT * FROM parquet.`/path`.
Option D (Parquet files have the ability to be optimized) — OPTIMIZE applies to Delta tables, not to Parquet files as a source format.
Option E (Parquet files will become Delta tables) — the source files are read, not converted; CTAS writes a new table and leaves the Parquet alone.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/external

question: A data engineer is running code in a Databricks Repo that is cloned from a central Git repository. A colleague of the data engineer informs them that changes have been made and synced to the central Git repository. The data engineer now needs to sync their Databricks Repo to get the changes from the central Git repository. Which of the following Git operations does the data engineer need to run to accomplish this task?
optionA: Merge
optionB: Push
optionC: Pull
optionD: Commit
optionE: Clone
explanation:
Pull is the Git operation that brings the central repository's changes into the Databricks Repo. It fetches the latest commits from the remote and merges them into the local branch, and can be run from the Pull button in the Repos UI or as git pull in a terminal session.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Merge) — combines two branches that are already local; it does not fetch anything from the remote.
Option B (Push) — sends local commits to the remote, the opposite direction.
Option D (Commit) — records changes to the local repository and touches the remote not at all.
Option E (Clone) — creates a new local copy of a remote repository; the engineer already has one.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/repos/git-operations-with-repos

question:
A data engineer has been given a new record of data:
```
id STRING = 'a1'
rank INTEGER = 6
rating FLOAT = 9.4
```
Which of the following SQL commands can be used to append the new record to an existing Delta table my_table?
optionA:
```sql
INSERT INTO my_table VALUES ('a1', 6, 9.4)
```
optionB:
```sql
my_table UNION VALUES ('a1', 6, 9.4)
```
optionC:
```sql
INSERT VALUES ( 'a1' , 6, 9.4) INTO my_table
```
optionD:
```sql
UPDATE my_table VALUES ('a1', 6, 9.4)
```
optionE:
```sql
UPDATE VALUES ('a1', 6, 9.4) my_table
```
explanation:
INSERT INTO my_table VALUES ('a1', 6, 9.4) is the statement that appends a row to an existing Delta table. INSERT INTO with a VALUES clause inserts one or more rows carrying the listed values, in column order.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (my_table UNION VALUES ...) — UNION is a query operator that returns a combined result set; it does not write to a table.
Option C (INSERT VALUES (...) INTO my_table) — not valid syntax; the table name comes before VALUES.
Option D (UPDATE my_table VALUES ...) — UPDATE modifies existing rows and has no VALUES clause; it cannot add a row.
Option E (UPDATE VALUES (...) my_table) — not valid syntax at all.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-dml-insert-into

question: What is the structure of an Asset Bundle?
optionA: A YAML configuration file that specifies the artifacts, resources, and configurations for the project.
optionB: A Docker image containing runtime environments and the source code of the assets
optionC: A single plain text file enumerating the names of assets to be migrated to a new workspace.
optionD: A compressed archive (ZIP) that solely contains workspace assets without any accompanying metadata.
explanation:
A YAML configuration file that specifies the artifacts, resources and configurations for the project is what an Asset Bundle is. The bundle's databricks.yml at the project root declares the bundle name, its targets (such as dev and prod), workspace settings, permissions, and the resources the project deploys, which is how jobs and pipelines get expressed as code and version-controlled alongside the source they run.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (a Docker image) — bundles are source-controlled configuration and code, not container images.
Option C (a plain text file listing asset names) — a bundle declares full resource definitions, not a bare list of names to migrate.
Option D (a ZIP of workspace assets without metadata) — the whole point of a bundle is that the metadata travels with the project in readable, reviewable configuration.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/bundles/

question: A data engineer is attempting to write Python and SQL in the same command cell and is running into an error. The engineer thought that it was possible to use a Python variable in a select statement. Why does the command fail?
optionA: Databricks supports language interoperability in the same cell but only between Scala and SQL
optionB: Databricks supports one language per cell.
optionC: Databricks supports multiple languages but only one per notebook.
optionD: Databricks supports language interoperability but only if a special character is used.
explanation:
Databricks supports one language per cell, which is why the command fails. The notebook has a default language, and a cell either inherits it or overrides it wholesale, either by picking a language from the cell's language button or by putting a %python, %sql, %r or %scala magic at the very beginning of the cell. Either way the whole cell is then that one language, so Python and SQL cannot be interleaved inside a single command cell.
The magic command is therefore not a way to mix two languages in one cell — it changes which single language that cell uses. To pass a Python variable into SQL, keep them in separate cells and use spark.sql() with an f-string, or a widget, rather than trying to write both languages together.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (interoperability only between Scala and SQL) — no language pair can share a cell; Scala is not special.
Option C (only one language per notebook) — a notebook mixes languages freely across cells via magics; the limit is per cell.
Option D (interoperability if a special character is used) — the % magic selects a cell's single language; it does not let two coexist.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/notebooks/notebooks-code

corrected.note: The documentation describes setting a notebook default language and overriding it per cell via the language button or a leading %<language> magic. The override applies to the entire cell, so the reason the command fails is one language per cell. The v2026-06-09 snapshot of this same item keys this option; the v2026-07-28 copy keyed the magic-character option.

question: Identify the impact of ON VIOLATION DROP ROW and ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE for a constraint violation. A data engineer has created an ETL pipeline using Delta Live table to manage their company travel reimbursement detail, they want to ensure that the if the location details has not been provided by the employee, the pipeline needs to be terminated. How can the scenario be implemented?
optionA:
```sql
CONSTRAINT valid_location EXPECT (location != NULL) ON VIOLATION FAIL
```
optionB:
```sql
CONSTRAINT valid_location EXPECT (location != NULL) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE
```
optionC:
```sql
CONSTRAINT valid_location EXPECT (location = NULL)
```
optionD:
```sql
CONSTRAINT valid_location EXPECT (location != NULL) ON DROP ROW
```
explanation:
CONSTRAINT valid_location EXPECT (location != NULL) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE is the clause that stops the pipeline when an employee has not supplied location details. FAIL UPDATE is the expectation action documented for that: "Invalid records prevent the update from succeeding. Manual intervention is required before reprocessing."
Two caveats about this item as printed. The valid SQL for a null test is location IS NOT NULL; location != NULL evaluates to NULL for every row and so never fires. And two of the distractors are not real syntax either — the documented forms are ON VIOLATION DROP ROW and ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE. Option B is right on the clause the question is testing, which is what the exam is asking.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (ON VIOLATION FAIL) — not documented syntax; the action is FAIL UPDATE.
Option C (EXPECT (location = NULL) with no action) — inverts the test and omits the action, leaving the default warn behaviour, which writes the record and only logs a metric.
Option D (ON DROP ROW) — not documented syntax, and even the real ON VIOLATION DROP ROW discards the row while the pipeline continues rather than terminating it.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectations

corrected.note: Answer stands. The expectations table documents ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE as the action that prevents the update from succeeding. Flagging that every option in this item uses != NULL, which is not a working null test in SQL; the item tests the ON VIOLATION clause, not the predicate.

question: A data engineer is maintaining an ETL pipeline code with a GitHub repository linked to their Databricks account. The data engineer wants to deploy the ETL pipeline to production as a databricks workflow. Which approach should the data engineer use?
optionA: Manually create and manage the workflow in Ul
optionB: Maintain workflow_conf ig. json and deploy it using Terraform
optionC: Maintain workflow_config.j son and deploy it using Databricks CLI
optionD: Databricks Asset Bundles (DAB) + GitHub Integration
explanation:
Databricks Asset Bundles (DAB) with the existing GitHub integration is the supported path from a Git-managed ETL repository to a production workflow. The job is declared in the bundle's YAML, lives in the same repository as the code it runs, and is deployed with the Databricks CLI — which a GitHub Actions workflow can invoke, so promotion to production is a reviewable commit rather than a manual step.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (manually create the workflow in the UI) — leaves production configuration undocumented and unreproducible.
Option B (workflow_config.json deployed with Terraform) — Terraform is legitimate for platform-level infrastructure, but a hand-maintained JSON for one pipeline reinvents what bundles standardise.
Option C (workflow_config.json deployed with the Databricks CLI) — the CLI is the right tool, but the bundle is the declared format it deploys; a bespoke JSON is not.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/bundles/
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/ci-cd

question: A data engineer has developed a data pipeline to ingest data from a JSON source using Auto Loader, but the engineer has not provided any type inference or schema hints in their pipeline. Upon reviewing the data, the data engineer has noticed that all of the columns in the target table are of the string type despite some of the fields only including float or boolean values. Which of the following describes why Auto Loader inferred all of the columns to be of the string type?
optionA: There was a type mismatch between the specific schema and the inferred schema
optionB: JSON data is a text-based format
optionC: Auto Loader only works with string data
optionD: All of the fields had at least one null value
optionE: Auto Loader cannot infer the schema of ingested data
explanation:
JSON data is a text-based format, and that is why Auto Loader inferred every column as a string. By default Auto Loader treats JSON columns as strings because the same field can carry different types across files or records, and it does not attempt to reconcile them — a column with integers in some files and strings in others would lose data if narrowed. The option that changes this is cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes: set to true, Auto Loader samples the data and infers integers, floats, booleans and nested structures; it defaults to false.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (type mismatch between specified and inferred schema) — no schema was specified, so there is nothing to mismatch.
Option C (Auto Loader only works with string data) — false; with inferColumnTypes or schema hints it produces typed columns.
Option D (all fields had at least one null) — nulls do not force a string type; the default string inference applies regardless.
Option E (Auto Loader cannot infer the schema) — it did infer one; the question is why the inferred types were strings.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ingestion/cloud-object-storage/auto-loader/schema

question: Which of the following describes a scenario in which a data engineer will want to use a single-node cluster?
optionA: When they are working interactively with a small amount of data
optionB: When they are running automated reports to be refreshed as quickly as possible
optionC: When they are working with SQL within Databricks SQL
optionD: When they are concerned about the ability to automatically scale with larger data
optionE: When they are manually running reports with a large amount of data
explanation:
Working interactively with a small amount of data is the scenario for a single-node cluster. A single-node cluster has a Spark driver and no workers, runs Spark locally with one executor thread per logical core, and is documented for lightweight exploratory data analysis and single-node machine learning workloads that use Spark to load and save data. It is created by choosing Single Node when configuring the cluster.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (automated reports refreshed as quickly as possible) — that calls for a multi-node cluster, ideally backed by a pool, so the work is distributed and start-up is short.
Option C (SQL within Databricks SQL) — Databricks SQL runs on SQL warehouses, not on an all-purpose single-node cluster.
Option D (concerned about scaling with larger data) — a single-node cluster cannot add workers; autoscaling needs a multi-node cluster.
Option E (manually running reports on a large amount of data) — large data needs the computation spread across workers.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/configure

question: A data engineer has a single-task Job that runs each morning before they begin working. After identifying an upstream data issue, they need to set up another task to run a new notebook prior to the original task. Which of the following approaches can the data engineer use to set up the new task?
optionA: They can clone the existing task in the existing Job and update it to run the new notebook.
optionB: They can create a new task in the existing Job and then add it as a dependency of the original task.
optionC: They can create a new task in the existing Job and then add the original task as a dependency of the new task.
optionD: They can create a new job from scratch and add both tasks to run concurrently.
optionE: They can clone the existing task to a new Job and then edit it to run the new notebook.
explanation:
Creating a new task in the existing Job and adding it as a dependency of the original task is the approach. In the Job, add a task that runs the new notebook, configured with its parameters; then edit the original task's Depends on setting to name the new task. The Job then runs the new notebook first and the original task only after it succeeds.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (clone the existing task and point it at the new notebook) — cloning gives a second task, but without a dependency nothing orders it before the original.
Option C (add the original task as a dependency of the new task) — that is the dependency backwards; the new notebook would run after the original.
Option D (new job with both tasks running concurrently) — concurrent execution does not guarantee the new notebook finishes before the original starts.
Option E (clone the task to a new Job) — a separate Job has no dependency link to the original task at all.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/configure-task

question: An organization plans to share a large dataset stored in a Databricks workspace on AWS with a partner organization whose Databricks workspace is hosted on Azure. The data engineer wants to minimize data transfer costs while ensuring secure and efficient data sharing. Which strategy will reduce data egress costs associated with cross-cloud data sharing?
optionA: Using Delta Sharing without any additional configurations
optionB: Configure VPN connection between AWS and Azure for faster data sharing
optionC: Sharing data via pre-signed URLs without monitoring egress costs
optionD: Migrating the dataset to Cloudflare R2 object storage before sharing
explanation:
Using Delta Sharing without any additional configuration keeps cross-cloud transfer costs down, because it does not copy the dataset. The provider shares a table in place and the recipient reads the underlying files directly from the provider's cloud storage using short-lived signed URLs, so no second copy is created and nothing is staged in an intermediate location — and the protocol works across clouds, which is exactly the AWS-to-Azure case here.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (VPN between AWS and Azure) — infrastructure to build and pay for, and it does not remove egress; bytes still leave AWS.
Option C (pre-signed URLs without monitoring egress) — hand-rolled sharing discards Unity Catalog's governance and auditing, and the option itself concedes egress goes unmonitored.
Option D (migrate the dataset to Cloudflare R2 first) — a full data movement, with its own egress, before any sharing has happened.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/opensharing

question: A data engineer needs to determine whether to use the built-in Databricks Notebooks versioning or version their project using Databricks Repos. Which of the following is an advantage of using Databricks Repos over the Databricks Notebooks versioning?
optionA: Databricks Repos automatically saves development progress
optionB: Databricks Repos supports the use of multiple branches
optionC: Databricks Repos allows users to revert to previous versions of a notebook
optionD: Databricks Repos provides the ability to comment on specific changes
optionE: Databricks Repos is wholly housed within the Databricks Lakehouse Platform
explanation:
Databricks Repos supports the use of multiple branches, and that is its advantage over the legacy notebook versioning. Repos (now Git folders) is a visual Git client in the workspace supporting clone, commit, push, pull and branch management, so a team can keep separate branches for features, experiments or fixes and merge, rebase or resolve conflicts between them. The legacy notebook versioning linked a single notebook to a Git repository and offered only basic commit and revert; it had no branch workflow.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (automatically saves development progress) — that is the notebook's own autosave and revision history, which both approaches have; it is not a Repos advantage.
Option C (revert to previous versions) — the legacy notebook versioning could already restore an earlier revision; reverting is not what distinguishes Repos.
Option D (comment on specific changes) — review comments live in the Git provider's pull requests, not in Repos itself.
Option E (wholly housed within the Databricks platform) — Repos exists precisely to integrate with an external Git provider; being self-contained is neither true nor an advantage.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/repos/

question: A data engineering team has noticed that their Databricks SQL queries are running too slowly when they are submitted to a non-running SQL endpoint. The data engineering team wants this issue to be resolved. Which of the following approaches can the team use to reduce the time it takes to return results in this scenario?
optionA: They can turn on the Serverless feature for the SQL endpoint and change the Spot Instance Policy to "Reliability Optimized."
optionB: They can turn on the Auto Stop feature for the SQL endpoint.
optionC: They can increase the cluster size of the SQL endpoint.
optionD: They can turn on the Serverless feature for the SQL endpoint.
optionE: They can increase the maximum bound of the SQL endpoint's scaling range
explanation:
Turning on the Serverless feature for the SQL endpoint is the fix for slow results against a non-running endpoint. The delay in that scenario is cold start — the time to bring up compute before the first query can run — and a serverless SQL warehouse starts in seconds from Databricks-managed capacity instead of provisioning instances in the customer's account. Serverless warehouses also scale up and down with query load, so concurrency improves as a side effect.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Serverless plus a "Reliability Optimized" spot policy) — a spot instance policy applies to classic warehouses that provision cloud instances; serverless compute has no spot setting, so the second half of the option is inapplicable.
Option B (Auto Stop) — stops an idle endpoint sooner, which makes the cold-start problem more frequent, not less.
Option C (increase the cluster size) — speeds up running queries but does nothing about the start-up wait before the endpoint is running.
Option E (raise the maximum scaling bound) — adds capacity for concurrent load; it does not shorten the time to start the first cluster.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/admin/sql/serverless

question: Which of the following SQL keywords can be used to convert a table from a long format to a wide format?
optionA: PIVOT
optionB: CONVERT
optionC: WHERE
optionD: TRANSFORM
optionE: SUM
explanation:
PIVOT is the SQL keyword that converts a table from long to wide format. The PIVOT clause rotates rows into columns: it aggregates one column's values grouped by the distinct values of another, and uses those distinct values as the new column names — sales by product and region as rows becoming one column per region, for instance.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (CONVERT) — a function that changes an expression's data type; it does not reshape rows into columns.
Option C (WHERE) — filters rows on a condition and leaves the shape of the table alone.
Option D (TRANSFORM) — applies a function to each element of an array (or, in Hive syntax, a script to rows); it is not a reshaping clause.
Option E (SUM) — an aggregate that PIVOT may use internally, but on its own it totals a column and produces no new columns.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-pivot

question: A data engineer manages multiple external tables linked to various data sources. The data engineer wants to manage these external tables efficiently and ensure that only the necessary permissions are granted to users for accessing specific external tables. How should the data engineer manage access to these external tables?
optionA: Use Unity Catalog to manage access controls and permissions for each external table individually.
optionB: Create a single user role with full access to all external tables and assign it to all users.
optionC: Grant permissions on the Databricks workspace level, which will automatically apply to all external tables.
optionD: Set up Azure Blob Storage permissions at the container level, allowing access to all external tables.
explanation:
Using Unity Catalog to manage access controls and permissions for each external table individually is how per-table access is done. Unity Catalog is the governance layer for external tables and grants privileges per securable object, so the engineer can hold SELECT on one external table without holding it on the next — which is what "only the necessary permissions" requires — and the grants are enforced consistently across every workspace attached to the metastore.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (single role with full access for all users) — the opposite of least privilege; every user reaches every table.
Option C (workspace-level permissions) — workspace permissions do not express table-level access and cannot restrict one table from another.
Option D (storage container permissions) — governs the files rather than the tables, losing per-table granularity and letting users reach the data outside Databricks where Unity Catalog cannot audit it.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/

question: A data engineer is using the following code block as part of a batch ingestion pipeline to read from a composable table: Which of the following changes needs to be made so this code block will work when the transactions table is a stream source?
optionA: Replace predict with a stream-friendly prediction function
optionB: Replace schema(schema) with option ("maxFilesPerTrigger", 1)
optionC: Replace "transactions" with the path to the location of the Delta table
optionD: Replace format("delta") with format("stream")
optionE: Replace spark.read with spark.readStream
explanation:
Replacing spark.read with spark.readStream is the change that makes the code block work against a stream source. spark.readStream returns a DataStreamReader, which accepts the same format, schema, path and option settings as the batch reader but produces a streaming DataFrame; spark.read is the batch entry point and cannot read a stream.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (replace predict with a stream-friendly function) — the transformation logic is unaffected by whether the source is batch or streaming.
Option B (replace schema(schema) with maxFilesPerTrigger) — a schema is still needed on a stream, and maxFilesPerTrigger is a rate-limiting option for file sources, not a replacement for one.
Option C (replace "transactions" with the table's path) — a Delta table can be read as a stream by name; the identifier is not the problem.
Option D (replace format("delta") with format("stream")) — "stream" is not a data source format; Delta is still the format, and streaming is selected by the reader, not the format string.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/structured-streaming/concepts

question: Which type of workloads are compatible with Auto Loader?
optionA: Streaming workloads
optionB: Machine learning workloads
optionC: Batch workloads
optionD: Serverless workloads
explanation:
Streaming workloads are what Auto Loader is compatible with. It provides a Structured Streaming source called cloudFiles that incrementally processes new files as they land in cloud object storage, tracking which files it has already seen so each one is handled exactly once without anyone maintaining a manifest.
Because it is a Structured Streaming source, a job can still be run on a schedule rather than continuously — Trigger.AvailableNow processes whatever has accumulated and then stops — but that is a triggering choice on a streaming query, not a separate batch mode.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (machine learning workloads) — Auto Loader is an ingestion source, not an ML feature; it says nothing about training or inference.
Option C (batch workloads) — Auto Loader is built on the streaming reader; a scheduled AvailableNow run is still a streaming query, not spark.read.
Option D (serverless workloads) — "serverless" describes compute, not a class of workload; Auto Loader runs on either compute type.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ingestion/cloud-object-storage/auto-loader/

question: Which of the following Git operations must be performed outside of Databricks Repos?
optionA: Commit
optionB: Pull
optionC: Push
optionD: Clone
optionE: Merge
explanation:
Merge is the answer this item is testing, and it reflects how Databricks Repos behaved when the feature was young: cloning, committing, pushing and pulling were available in the workspace, while merging a branch had to be done in the Git provider's own interface.
Be aware that current Databricks Git folders have moved on. The documentation now lists Merge branches, Resolve merge conflicts, Rebase a branch and Reset a branch among the supported Git-folder operations, so on a current workspace none of the five listed operations strictly requires leaving Databricks. Merge remains the best answer to the question as written, but treat it as the historical answer rather than a present-day limitation.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Commit) — always available in the Repos dialog.
Option B (Pull) — always available in the Repos dialog.
Option C (Push) — always available in the Repos dialog.
Option D (Clone) — adding a repo to the workspace is a clone, performed inside Databricks.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/repos/git-operations-with-repos

corrected.note: Answer kept as the legacy exam key. Current documentation lists merge, rebase and conflict resolution as supported inside Git folders, so the premise of the question is now stale; flagged rather than silently confirmed.

question: A data engineer has been using a Databricks SQL dashboard to monitor the cleanliness of the input data to a data analytics dashboard for a retail use case. The job has a Databricks SQL query that returns the number of store-level records where sales is equal to zero. The data engineer wants their entire team to be notified via a messaging webhook whenever this value is greater than 0. Which of the following approaches can the data engineer use to notify their entire team via a messaging webhook whenever the number of stores with $0 in sales is greater than zero?
optionA: They can set up an Alert with a custom template.
optionB: They can set up an Alert with a new email alert destination.
optionC: They can set up an Alert with one-time notifications.
optionD: They can set up an Alert with a new webhook alert destination.
optionE: They can set up an Alert without notifications.
explanation:
Setting up an Alert with a new webhook alert destination is how the whole team gets notified over a messaging webhook. A webhook notification destination makes Databricks send an HTTP POST to a third-party endpoint when the alert fires, which is how Slack, Microsoft Teams or PagerDuty integrations are built: create the webhook connector in the messaging platform, register its URL as a Databricks notification destination, then create an alert on the SQL query with the condition "value > 0" and pick that destination. The alert can run on a schedule and carries a custom message template and a link back to the query.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an Alert with a custom template) — a template shapes the message body; it does not choose where the message goes.
Option B (a new email alert destination) — delivers by email, not through the messaging webhook the team asked for.
Option C (an Alert with one-time notifications) — the team wants to be told whenever the value is greater than 0, which needs recurring notification, not a single one.
Option E (an Alert without notifications) — an alert that notifies no one does not meet the requirement.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/user/alerts/

question: Which of the following data lakehouse features results in improved data quality over a traditional data lake?
optionA: A data lakehouse provides storage solutions for structured and unstructured data.
optionB: A data lakehouse supports ACID-compliant transactions.
optionC: A data lakehouse allows the use of SQL queries to examine data.
optionD: A data lakehouse stores data in open formats.
optionE: A data lakehouse enables machine learning and artificial Intelligence workloads.
explanation:
Supporting ACID-compliant transactions is the lakehouse feature that improves data quality over a traditional data lake. A lakehouse combines the flexibility, cost and scale of a data lake with the data management guarantees of a warehouse, and the transactional layer (Delta Lake) is what ensures integrity, consistency and isolation across concurrent reads and writes. A plain data lake has no transactions, so concurrent or streaming ingestion can leave corrupted, duplicated or partially written data behind.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (storage for structured and unstructured data) — a traditional data lake already does this; it is not what improves quality.
Option C (SQL queries to examine data) — query access is a convenience for consumers and does nothing to prevent bad or inconsistent writes.
Option D (open formats) — data lakes also store open formats such as Parquet; the format alone carries no integrity guarantee.
Option E (ML and AI workloads) — an outcome the lakehouse enables, not a mechanism that makes the data itself more reliable.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/delta/

question:
A data engineer needs to create a table in Databricks using data from a CSV file at location /path/to/csv. They run the following command:
```sql
CREATE TABLE new_table
_____
OPTIONS (
  header = "true",
  delimiter = "|"
)
LOCATION "path/to/csv"
```
Which of the following lines of code fills in the above blank to successfully complete the task?
optionA: USING DELTA
optionB: FROM CSV
optionC: None of these lines of code are needed to successfully complete the task
optionD: FROM "path/to/csv"
optionE: USING CSV
explanation:
USING CSV completes the statement. In CREATE TABLE the USING clause names the file format the table is backed by, so USING CSV tells Databricks to read the files at the given location as CSV, with the OPTIONS clause supplying the header and delimiter settings.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (USING DELTA) — declares the wrong format for a CSV source; the files at the location are not Delta.
Option B (FROM CSV) — FROM belongs in a SELECT, not in a table definition.
Option C (none needed) — without USING the table falls back to the default format rather than reading the CSV data as intended.
Option D (FROM "path/to/csv") — query syntax again, and the location is already supplied by the statement's LOCATION clause.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-create-table-using

question: Which tool is used by Auto Loader to process data incrementally?
optionA: Spark Structured Streaming
optionB: Unity Catalog
optionC: Checkpointing
optionD: Databricks SQL
explanation:
Spark Structured Streaming is the tool Auto Loader uses to process data incrementally. Auto Loader is exposed as the cloudFiles Structured Streaming source; the streaming engine is what discovers new files as they arrive in cloud storage, processes only what has not yet been seen, and supports the schema inference and file notification mode that make it work on a changing data lake.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Unity Catalog) — the governance layer for data and permissions; it does not drive ingestion.
Option C (Checkpointing) — a mechanism Structured Streaming uses to record progress, not the processing engine itself.
Option D (Databricks SQL) — the warehouse and query interface; Auto Loader is not run from it.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ingestion/cloud-object-storage/auto-loader/

question: Which two components function in the DB platform architecture's control plane? (Choose two.)
optionA: Compute Orchestration
optionB: Unity Catalog
optionC: Virtual Machines
optionD: Compute
optionE: Serverless Compute
explanation:
Compute Orchestration and Unity Catalog both run in the control plane. The control plane holds the backend services Databricks manages in its own account — the web application, the service that schedules and orchestrates compute, and the Unity Catalog metastore that governs data across workspaces.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (Virtual Machines) — the instances that run workloads, in the compute plane (the customer's cloud account for classic compute).
Option D (Compute) — the processing resources themselves; compute plane, not control plane.
Option E (Serverless Compute) — the same processing role, just run in a Databricks-managed serverless compute plane; still the compute plane. The dividing line is management versus processing, not who pays for it.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/getting-started/overview

question: Which of the following must be specified when creating a new Delta Live Tables pipeline?
optionA: A key-value pair configuration
optionB: The preferred DBU/hour cost
optionC: A path to cloud storage location for the written data
optionD: A location of a target database for the written data
optionE: At least one notebook library to be executed
explanation:
At least one notebook library to be executed is the one thing that must be specified when creating a Delta Live Tables pipeline. A pipeline is a data processing workflow made of materialized views and streaming tables declared in Python or SQL source files; DLT infers the dependencies between them and runs updates in the right order. Without a source file there is nothing to run, and the create-pipeline dialog will not proceed without one. Several libraries, in either language, may be added.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a key-value pair configuration) — optional; used to customise settings such as storage location, target schema, notifications or pipeline mode.
Option B (the preferred DBU/hour cost) — not a pipeline setting at all; cost follows from the cluster configuration.
Option C (a cloud storage path for the written data) — optional; if left empty the system uses a default location.
Option D (a target database) — optional; a target schema in the Hive metastore or Unity Catalog can be set, but the pipeline can be created without one.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/configure-pipeline

question: A data engineer needs to combine sales data from an on-premises PostgreSQL database with customer data in Azure Synapse for a comprehensive report. The goal is to avoid data duplication and ensure up-to-date information. How should the data engineer achieve this using Databricks?
optionA: Export data from both sources to CSV files and upload them to Databricks
optionB: Develop custom ETL pipelines to ingest data into Databricks
optionC: Manually synchronize data from both sources into a single database
optionD: Use Lakehouse Federation to query both data sources directly
explanation:
Using Lakehouse Federation to query both data sources directly lets Databricks read the PostgreSQL and Synapse data where it already lives. A connection and a foreign catalog are registered for each source, their tables become queryable through Unity Catalog, and a single query can join across them — so there is no copy to fall out of date and no duplication, which is precisely what the question asks for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (export both to CSV and upload) — a snapshot that is stale the moment it is written, and a second copy of the data.
Option B (custom ETL pipelines into Databricks) — creates and then has to maintain a duplicate copy.
Option C (manually synchronise into a single database) — the same duplication done by hand, with more room for drift.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/query-federation/

question: A new data engineering team has been assigned to work on a project. The team will need access to database customers in order to see what tables already exist. The team has its own group team. Which of the following commands can be used to grant the necessary permission on the entire database to the new team?
explanation:
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE customers TO team; is the command that lets the team see which tables exist in the database. Listing a container's contents requires the privilege that lets a principal traverse into it, and USAGE is that privilege in the legacy Hive metastore model.
One currency note: USAGE ON DATABASE is the legacy Hive metastore spelling. Under Unity Catalog the equivalent privileges are USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA, granted as GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA <catalog>.<schema> TO <principal>, with SELECT needed additionally to read the data itself. The concept is unchanged: a traversal privilege on the container, separate from any privilege on its contents.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (GRANT VIEW ON CATALOG customers TO team) — VIEW is not a privilege, and customers is a database here, not a catalog.
Option B (GRANT CREATE ON DATABASE customers TO team) — CREATE allows making new objects, not listing existing ones.
Option C (GRANT USAGE ON CATALOG team TO customers) — inverts principal and securable, granting to customers on an object called team.
Option D (GRANT CREATE ON DATABASE team TO customers) — the wrong privilege and the wrong direction at once.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/access-control/privileges-reference

corrected.note: Answer stands. Added the Unity Catalog equivalent (USE CATALOG / USE SCHEMA) because USAGE ON DATABASE is legacy Hive metastore syntax and a learner on a current workspace will not find USAGE in the privilege list.

question: A departing platform owner currently holds ownership of multiple catalogs and controls storage credentials and external locations. The data engineer wants to ensure continuity: transfer catalog ownership to the platform team group, delegate ongoing privilege management, and retain the ability to receive and share data via Delta Sharing. Which role must be in place to perform these actions across the metastore?
optionA: Account Admin, because account admins can only create metastores but cannot change ownership of catalogs.
optionB: Workspace Admin, because workspace admins can transfer ownership of any Unity Catalog object.
optionC: Metastore Admin, because metastore admins can transfer ownership and manage privileges across all metastore objects, including shares and recipients.
optionD: Catalog Owner, because catalog owners can transfer any object in any catalog in the metastore.
explanation:
Metastore Admin is the role that can transfer catalog ownership, manage privileges across every securable in the metastore, and administer storage credentials, external locations and Delta Sharing objects such as shares and recipients. It is the highest authority within a metastore, which is what continuity across all of a departing owner's catalogs needs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Account Admin) — operates at the account level, creating metastores and assigning metastore admins; it is not the role for day-to-day ownership and privilege management inside an existing metastore, and the option's own reasoning concedes it cannot change catalog ownership.
Option B (Workspace Admin) — manages workspace-level settings and has no authority over Unity Catalog ownership unless explicitly granted it.
Option D (Catalog Owner) — scoped to a single catalog; cannot act across every catalog, credential and share in the metastore.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/manage-privileges/admin-privileges

question: In which of the following scenarios should a data engineer use the MERGE INTO command instead of the INSERT INTO command?
optionA: When the location of the data needs to be changed
optionB: When the target table is an external table
optionC: When the source table can be deleted
optionD: When the target table cannot contain duplicate records
optionE: When the source is not a Delta table
explanation:
When the target table cannot contain duplicate records is the scenario for MERGE INTO. MERGE performs an upsert: it matches source rows to target rows on a merge condition and then updates the matches, inserts the new rows, or deletes as instructed — so a row that already exists is updated in place rather than appended a second time. INSERT INTO only appends, and would create the duplicate.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the location of the data needs to be changed) — moving data between tables or partitions is a plain INSERT INTO ... SELECT; no matching is involved.
Option B (the target is an external table) — INSERT INTO writes to external tables perfectly well; the table type does not decide between the two commands.
Option C (the source table can be deleted) — whether the source is disposable (a temp view, say) is irrelevant to how rows land in the target.
Option E (the source is not a Delta table) — INSERT INTO accepts Parquet, CSV, JSON or any readable source; MERGE is chosen for the target's uniqueness requirement, not the source's format.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/delta-merge-into

question: A data engineer has three tables in a Delta Live Tables (DLT) pipeline. They have configured the pipeline to drop invalid records at each table. They notice that some data is being dropped due to quality concerns at some point in the DLT pipeline. They would like to determine at which table in their pipeline the data is being dropped. Which of the following approaches can the data engineer take to identify the table that is dropping the records?
optionA: They can set up separate expectations for each table when developing their DLT pipeline.
optionB: They cannot determine which table is dropping the records.
optionC: They can set up DLT to notify them via email when records are dropped.
optionD: They can navigate to the DLT pipeline page, click on each table, and view the data quality statistics.
optionE: They can navigate to the DLT pipeline page, click on the "Error" button, and review the present errors.
explanation:
Navigating to the DLT pipeline page, clicking on each table and viewing the data quality statistics is how the engineer finds where records are being dropped. DLT records data quality metrics per dataset — records passing and failing each expectation, records dropped, records written — and the pipeline UI shows them for the latest update or any previous one, table by table.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (set up separate expectations for each table) — the pipeline already has expectations at each table; the question is how to read the results, not how to add more.
Option B (cannot determine which table) — false; the per-table metrics exist for exactly this purpose.
Option C (email notification when records are dropped) — pipeline notifications cover update success, failure and flow progress; they do not say which table dropped rows.
Option E (the "Error" button) — dropped rows are not errors; a DROP ROW expectation succeeds by design, so nothing appears in the error view.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectations

question: A team creates YAML manifests that declare jobs, resources, and dependencies, then deploys them to Databricks using the Databricks CLI. The deployment succeeds. Which feature are they using?
optionA: Databricks Asset Bundles
optionB: GitHub
optionC: Terraform
optionD: DataOps
explanation:
Databricks Asset Bundles are the feature described: YAML manifests declaring jobs, resources and dependencies, deployed with the Databricks CLI. A bundle has a required databricks.yml at its root, declares resources such as jobs and pipelines, artifacts and deployment targets, and is validated, deployed and run with the CLI — which standardises how workflows are packaged and promoted across dev, test and prod while keeping the definitions version-controlled.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (GitHub) — a hosting and version-control platform where the YAML might live; it does not deploy anything to Databricks.
Option C (Terraform) — a separate infrastructure-as-code tool with its own HCL language and provider, not YAML deployed through the Databricks CLI.
Option D (DataOps) — a methodology, not a Databricks feature.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/bundles/

question:
A data engineer has joined an existing project and they see the following query in the project repository:
```sql
CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE loyal_customers AS
SELECT customer_id
FROM STREAM(LIVE.customers)
WHERE loyalty_level = 'high';
```
Which of the following describes why the STREAM function is included in the query?
optionA: The STREAM function is not needed and will cause an error.
optionB: The table being created is a live table.
optionC: The customers table is a streaming live table.
optionD: The customers table is a reference to a Structured Streaming query on a PySpark DataFrame.
optionE: The data in the customers table has been updated since its last run.
explanation:
The customers table is a streaming live table, which is why STREAM(LIVE.customers) appears in the query. The STREAM function reads a streaming table or view incrementally — only the records added since the last pipeline update — so loyal_customers can itself be declared as a streaming table that processes new high-loyalty customers as they arrive rather than recomputing the whole source.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (not needed and will cause an error) — STREAM is the documented way to consume a streaming table incrementally; it is required for that, not an error.
Option B (the table being created is a live table) — the target's own declaration is CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE; STREAM describes how the source is read, not what the target is.
Option D (a Structured Streaming query on a PySpark DataFrame) — this is SQL inside a DLT pipeline reading a pipeline dataset, not a reference to a PySpark object.
Option E (the data has been updated since the last run) — STREAM is a declaration of how to read the source on every update, not a statement about whether new data exists right now.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/concepts/flows

question:
Identify how the count_if function and the count where x is null can be used. Consider a table random_values with below data. What would be the output of below query?
```
select count_if(col > 1) as count_a, count(*) as count_b, count(col1) as count_c from random_values
```
col1: 0, 1, 2, NULL, 2, 3
explanation:
3 6 5 is the result, and each column is worth stepping through against the values 0, 1, 2, NULL, 2, 3.
count_if(col1 > 1) counts rows where the predicate is true: 2, 2 and 3 qualify, so 3. Note that the NULL row does not qualify — NULL > 1 evaluates to NULL rather than true, so it is not counted.
count(*) counts rows regardless of content, including the NULL row, so 6.
count(col1) counts non-null values in that column, which excludes the NULL, so 5. That difference between count(*) and count(column) is the point of the question: the first counts rows, the second counts values.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (4 6 5) — 4 would require the NULL row to satisfy col1 > 1, and a NULL comparison never evaluates to true.
Option B (3 6 6) — 6 for count(col1) would mean the NULL was counted as a value; count(column) skips nulls.
Option C (4 6 6) — wrong on both counts above.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/functions/count_if

question: A data engineer is processing ingested streaming tables and needs to filter out NULL values in the order_datetime column from the raw streaming table orders_raw, and store the results in a new table orders_valid using DLT. Which code snippet should the data engineer use?
optionA:
```sql
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE orders_valid(
  CONSTRAINT valid_date
  EXPECT (order_datetime IS NOT NULL)
  ON VIOLATION DROP ROW
)
AS SELECT * FROM STREAM orders_raw;
```
optionB:
```sql
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE orders_valid
AS
SELECT *
FROM STREAM(orders_raw)
WHERE order_datetime IS NOT NULL
```
optionC:
```sql
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE orders_valid
(
  CONSTRAINT valid_date EXPECT (order_datetime IS NOT NULL)
  ON VIOLATION DROP ROW
)
AS SELECT * FROM orders_raw;
```
optionD:
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAMING TABLE orders_valid
(
  FILTER (order_datetime IS NOT NULL)
)
AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(orders_raw);
```
explanation:
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE orders_valid with CONSTRAINT valid_date EXPECT (order_datetime IS NOT NULL) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW, reading AS SELECT * FROM STREAM orders_raw, is the snippet. Expectations are the documented Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines mechanism for filtering invalid records, and ON VIOLATION DROP ROW drops violating rows before the write while logging the dropped count alongside other dataset metrics. Reading the source with STREAM is what a streaming table needs.
One caveat worth knowing: option B does technically produce the same rows, because a WHERE clause on a streaming read also removes the NULLs. It is not the mechanism this question is testing, and it discards the data-quality metrics that expectations record, but the item would be stronger if B were not also workable.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (WHERE order_datetime IS NOT NULL) — filters the rows but records no data-quality metrics; not the expectations mechanism the question is about.
Option C (same constraint, AS SELECT * FROM orders_raw) — reads the source without STREAM, a batch read against a streaming source.
Option D (FILTER (order_datetime IS NOT NULL)) — FILTER is not an expectations clause; it is not valid in this position.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectations

corrected.note: The documentation names expectations with ON VIOLATION DROP ROW as the way to drop invalid records in a pipeline. The other scraped snapshot of this same question keys the expectations option, which agrees. Flagging that option B is also functionally valid, so this item has two workable answers and is weak.

question: A data engineer at a company that uses Databricks with Unity Catalog needs to share a collection of tables with an external partner who also uses a Databricks workspace enabled for Unity Catalog. The data engineer decides to use Delta Sharing to accomplish this. What is the first piece of information the data engineer should request from the external partner to set up Delta Sharing?
optionA: The IP address of their Databricks workspace
optionB: The sharing identifier of their Unity Catalog metastore
optionC: The name of their Databricks cluster
optionD: Their Databricks account password
explanation:
The sharing identifier of their Unity Catalog metastore is the first thing to request. In Databricks-to-Databricks sharing the provider creates a recipient object, and that recipient is identified by the consumer's metastore sharing identifier — a string of the form cloud:region:metastore-uuid. Without it the provider cannot create a recipient to share with.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (the IP address of their workspace) — plays no part in Delta Sharing's identity model.
Option C (the name of their cluster) — irrelevant; shares are addressed to a metastore, not to compute.
Option D (their account password) — should never be requested by anyone; Delta Sharing is designed so that no credential changes hands.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/opensharing/share-data-databricks

question: A data engineering team has two tables. The first table march_transactions is a collection of all retail transactions in the month of March. The second table april_transactions is a collection of all retail transactions in the month of April. There are no duplicate records between the tables. Which of the following commands should be run to create a new table all_transactions that contains all records from march_transactions and april_transactions without duplicate records?
optionA:
```sql
CREATE TABLE all_transactions AS
SELECT * FROM march_transactions
INNER JOIN SELECT * FROM april_transactions;
```
optionB:
```sql
CREATE TABLE all_transactions AS
SELECT * FROM march_transactions
UNION SELECT * FROM april_transactions;
```
optionC:
```sql
CREATE TABLE all_transactions AS
SELECT * FROM march_transactions
OUTER JOIN SELECT * FROM april_transactions;
```
optionD:
```sql
CREATE TABLE all_transactions AS
SELECT * FROM march_transactions
INTERSECT SELECT * from april_transactions;
```
optionE:
```sql
CREATE TABLE all_transactions AS
SELECT * FROM march_transactions
MERGE SELECT * FROM april_transactions;
```
explanation:
UNION is the operator that combines all rows from march_transactions and april_transactions without duplicates: it stacks the two result sets and removes duplicate rows (UNION ALL would keep them). CREATE TABLE all_transactions AS SELECT ... UNION SELECT ... therefore produces exactly the combined table asked for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (INNER JOIN) — a join matches rows across the tables on a condition and widens them; it does not stack one table under the other, and the printed syntax has no ON clause.
Option C (OUTER JOIN) — the same problem; joins combine columns, not rows.
Option D (INTERSECT) — returns only the rows present in both tables, which here is none.
Option E (MERGE) — not a set operator; MERGE INTO is an upsert statement with its own syntax and cannot sit between two SELECTs.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-setops

question: A data engineer needs access to a table new_uable, but they do not have the correct permissions. They can ask the table owner for permission, but they do not know who the table owner is. Which approach can be used to identify the owner of new_table?
optionA: There is no way to identify the owner of the table
optionB: Review the Owner field in the table ' s page in the cloud storage solution
optionC: Review the Permissions tab in the table ' s page in Data Explorer
optionD: Review the Owner field in the table's page in Data Explorer
explanation:
Reviewing the Owner field in the table's page in Data Explorer (now Catalog Explorer) identifies the table owner. Catalog Explorer shows the details of every data object, and a table's page carries an Owner field naming the user or group that owns it — the principal to ask for permission.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (no way to identify the owner) — false; ownership is a first-class property shown in the UI.
Option B (the Owner field in cloud storage) — the cloud storage console shows who owns the files or bucket, not the Unity Catalog table object.
Option C (the Permissions tab) — lists the privileges granted on the table, which does not necessarily name the owner.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/discover/database-objects

question: An organization is looking for an optimized storage layer that supports ACID transactions and schema enforcement. Which technology should the organization use?
optionA: Delta Lake
optionB: Data lake
optionC: Unity Catalog
optionD: Cloud File Storage
explanation:
Delta Lake is the optimized storage layer that provides ACID transactions and schema enforcement. Databricks documents it as the default storage format for all tables: an open-source layer that adds a transaction log over files in the object store, which is what makes atomic commits and schema enforcement possible on data sitting in cloud storage.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Data lake) — the thing Delta Lake improves on: raw files in object storage with no transaction log, so neither ACID guarantees nor schema enforcement.
Option C (Unity Catalog) — the governance layer, handling access control and lineage rather than storage.
Option D (Cloud File Storage) — the underlying object store the other layers sit on; it offers no transactions of its own.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/delta/

corrected.note: The question asks for a storage layer providing ACID transactions and schema enforcement, which is the definition of Delta Lake. The old key named the data lake, which is precisely the technology that lacks both properties.

question: A data engineer streams customer orders into a Kafka topic (orders_topic) and is currently writing the ingestion script of a DLT pipeline. The data engineer needs to ingest the data from Kafka brokers to DLT using Databricks. What is the correct code for ingesting the data?
optionA:
```sql
CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE orders_raw
AS SELECT
    value:order_id AS order_id,
    value:customer_id AS customer_id,
    value:amount AS amount,
    value:order_status AS order_status,
    value:order_timestamp AS order_timestamp
FROM cloud_files("kafka://broker:9092/orders_topic", "json");
```
optionB:
```sql
CREATE LIVE TABLE orders_raw
AS SELECT
    CAST(value AS STRING) AS json_data
FROM STREAM kafka.`broker:9092/orders_topic`;
```
optionD:
```sql
CREATE LIVE TABLE orders_raw
AS SELECT
    CAST(value AS STRING) AS json_data
FROM STREAM kafka.`broker:9092/orders_topic`;
```
explanation:
The Python snippet with @dlt.table returning spark.readStream.format("kafka") is the correct ingestion code. Kafka is not a cloud-storage source, so it is read with Spark Structured Streaming inside a Python pipeline rather than declared in SQL: import dlt, decorate the function with @dlt.table, and return the standard Kafka reader configured with kafka.bootstrap.servers, subscribe and startingOffsets, so the pipeline manages the resulting table.
A defect worth knowing about this item: two of its four options are the same text, so it presents three distinct choices rather than four.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (cloud_files("kafka://...", "json")) — cloud_files() is Auto Loader, which reads files from object storage, not a Kafka broker.
Option B (CREATE LIVE TABLE ... FROM STREAM kafka.`...`) — CREATE LIVE TABLE declares a materialised view recomputed from its source, when a continuously arriving Kafka topic needs a streaming table; and kafka.`broker` is not a DLT SQL source.
Option D (identical to option B) — the same text, and wrong for the same reasons.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/structured-streaming/concepts

question: A Data Engineer is building a simple data pipeline using Delta Live Tables (DLT) in Databricks to ingest customer data. The raw customer data is stored in a cloud storage location in JSON format. The task is to create a DLT pipeline that reads the raw JSON data and writes it into a Delta table for further processing. Which code snippet will correctly ingest the raw JSON data and create a Delta table using DLT?
explanation:
@dlt.table over spark.read.json("s3://my-bucket/raw-customers/") is the snippet. spark.read.json() is the reader that matches JSON source data, and wrapping it in @dlt.table declares the result as a table in the pipeline, which is what the question asks for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (spark.read.format("csv")) — reads the JSON files as CSV and would misparse them.
Option C (spark.read.format("parquet")) — reads them as Parquet, which fails outright on JSON text.
Option D (@dlt.view with spark.format.json) — wrong twice over: spark.format.json() is not a real method (the reader is reached through spark.read), and @dlt.view declares a view rather than the Delta table the task calls for.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/

question: A data engineer has a Job with multiple tasks that runs nightly. Each of the tasks runs slowly because the clusters take a long time to start. Which of the following actions can the data engineer perform to improve the start up time for the clusters used for the Job?
optionA: They can use endpoints available in Databricks SQL
optionB: They can use jobs clusters instead of all-purpose clusters
optionC: They can configure the clusters to be single-node
optionD: They can use clusters that are from a cluster pool
optionE: They can configure the clusters to autoscale for larger data sizes
explanation:
Using clusters from a cluster pool is the action that improves start-up time. A pool keeps a set of idle, ready-to-use instances, so a job cluster drawn from it skips the cloud provisioning wait that makes a cold cluster slow to start. Pools are shared across jobs and users, and Databricks does not bill DBUs for instances idling in the pool.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Databricks SQL endpoints) — serve SQL warehouse workloads; they do not change how a Job's clusters start.
Option B (jobs clusters instead of all-purpose) — both types provision instances the same way and start in similar time; the choice affects cost and isolation, not start-up.
Option C (single-node clusters) — cuts parallelism and does not shorten the instance provisioning wait.
Option E (autoscale for larger data) — adjusts worker count during a run; it does nothing before the cluster exists.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/pool-index

question: A data engineer is writing a script that is meant to ingest new data from cloud storage. In the event of the Schema change, the ingestion should fail. It should fail until the changes downstream source can be found and verified as intended changes. Which command will meet the requirements?
optionA: addNewColumns
optionB: none
optionC: failOnNewColumns
optionD: rescue
explanation:
failOnNewColumns is the schema-evolution mode that stops and stays stopped. Databricks documents it as failing the stream and not restarting unless you update the provided schema or remove the offending file, which is exactly the requirement here: halt on a schema change and keep halting until a human has confirmed the upstream change was intended.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (addNewColumns) — the default and the close distractor: it also fails the stream, but adds the new columns to the schema first, so a restart simply resumes with the changed schema and the unverified change flows through.
Option B (none) — silently ignores new columns, the worst outcome for a pipeline that is supposed to catch this.
Option D (rescue) — never fails at all; it routes unexpected columns into the rescued data column.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ingestion/cloud-object-storage/auto-loader/schema

question: Which of the following describes when to use the CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE (formerly CREATE INCREMENTAL LIVE TABLE) syntax over the CREATE LIVE TABLE syntax when creating Delta Live Tables (DLT) tables using SQL?
optionA: CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE should be used when the subsequent step in the DLT pipeline is static.
optionB: CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE should be used when data needs to be processed incrementally.
optionC: CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE is redundant for DLT and it does not need to be used.
optionD: CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE should be used when data needs to be processed through complicated aggregations.
optionE: CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE should be used when the previous step in the DLT pipeline is static.
explanation:
CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE should be used when data needs to be processed incrementally.
