A streaming table processes only the data added since the last pipeline update and is stateful: if the defining query changes, new data is processed under the new query and existing data is not recomputed. That fits streaming sources and incremental loads from append-only batch sources. A live table (materialized view), by contrast, may be recomputed in full, which suits complex transformations or aggregations that need to scan everything.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (when the subsequent step is static) — what comes after a table does not decide how it is defined; a streaming table can feed a materialized view.
Option C (redundant, need not be used) — false; it is the only way to get incremental, append-only processing in DLT SQL.
Option D (complicated aggregations) — that is the case for a live table, which can recompute the full result.
Option E (when the previous step is static) — a streaming table reads from an append-only source; a static upstream is the case for a live table.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/concepts/streaming-tables

question:
A data engineer has a Python variable table_name that they would like to use in a SQL query. They want to construct a Python code block that will run the query using table_name. They have the following incomplete code block:
```python
____(f"SELECT customer_id, spend FROM {table_name}")
```
Which of the following can be used to fill in the blank to successfully complete the task?
optionA: spark.delta.sql
optionB: spark.delta.table
optionC: spark.table
optionD: dbutils.sql
optionE: spark.sql
explanation:
spark.sql is the method that fills the blank. It executes a SQL statement passed as a string and returns the result as a DataFrame, so an f-string that interpolates the Python variable table_name is a natural fit: spark.sql(f"SELECT customer_id, spend FROM {table_name}").
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (spark.delta.sql) — not a real API; there is no spark.delta namespace.
Option B (spark.delta.table) — not a real API either.
Option C (spark.table) — takes a table name and returns that table as a DataFrame; it does not run a SQL statement.
Option D (dbutils.sql) — dbutils has no sql module; its utilities cover files, secrets, widgets and notebooks.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/pyspark/basics

question: A new data engineering team team has been assigned to an ELT project. The new data engineering team will need full privileges on the table sales to fully manage the project. Which of the following commands can be used to grant full permissions on the database to the new data engineering team?
explanation:
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON TABLE sales TO team; grants the team every privilege that applies to the table — SELECT and MODIFY on the table itself, plus whatever else the model allows on that securable — which is what "full privileges to fully manage the project" asks for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (GRANT SELECT CREATE MODIFY) — privileges must be comma-separated, and CREATE is not a table privilege; even read as intended it is a subset, not full access.
Option C (GRANT SELECT) — read access only, not enough to manage the table.
Option D (GRANT USAGE ON TABLE) — USAGE is a container privilege for schemas and catalogs; it is not valid on a table.
Option E (GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON TABLE team TO sales) — inverts securable and principal, granting on a table called team to a principal called sales.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/access-control/privileges-reference

question: A data engineer is inspecting an ETL pipeline based on a Pyspark job that consistently encounters performance bottlenecks. Based on developer feedback, the data engineer assumes the job is low on compute resources. To pinpoint the issue, the data engineer observes the Spark Ul and finds out the job has a high CPU time vs Task time. Which course of action should the data engineer take?
optionA: High CPU time vs Task time means an under-utilized cluster. The data engineer may need to repartition data to spread the jobs more evenly throughout the cluster.
optionB: High CPU time vs Task time means over-utilized memory and the need to increase parallelism
optionC: High CPU time vs Task time means a CPU over-utilized job. The data engineer may need to consider executor and core tuning or resizing the cluster
optionD: High CPU time vs Task time means efficient use of cluster and no change needed
explanation:
High CPU time versus task time means a CPU over-utilized job, so the engineer should consider executor and core tuning or resizing the cluster. Task time is how long a task took end to end; CPU time is how much of that the executor spent actually computing. When CPU time accounts for most of task time, the cores are busy rather than idle, so the stage is compute-bound and the remedy is more or faster CPU: tune the executor and core counts, or move to a larger or Photon-enabled cluster.
A caveat on this item: Databricks documents cluster CPU utilization as a metric and publishes a Spark UI diagnosis guide, but it does not publish this specific CPU-time-versus-task-time rule of thumb. The reasoning above follows from what the two metrics measure rather than from a documented Databricks statement.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (under-utilized cluster; repartition) — an under-utilized cluster shows CPU time far below task time, because tasks wait on I/O, shuffle or skew rather than computing; repartitioning helps that case, not this one.
Option B (over-utilized memory; increase parallelism) — memory pressure shows up as spill and GC time, not as elevated CPU time.
Option D (efficient use, no change needed) — a high ratio is not by itself proof of an efficient job; a slow UDF or an exploding join burns CPU productively-looking but pointlessly.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/cluster-metrics
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/optimizations/spark-ui-guide/

corrected.note: Answer stands as the best-supported option, but flagging that Databricks does not document this heuristic. Its Spark UI guide diagnoses slow stages by I/O, small files, skew, spill and slow UDFs, and never frames a CPU-time to task-time ratio. Treat this item as reasoning from metric definitions, not from vendor guidance.

question: A single Job runs two notebooks as two separate tasks. A data engineer has noticed that one of the notebooks is running slowly in the Job's current run. The data engineer asks a tech lead for help in identifying why this might be the case. Which of the following approaches can the tech lead use to identify why the notebook is running slowly as part of the Job?
optionA: They can navigate to the Tasks tab in the Jobs UI to immediately review the processing notebook.
optionB: They can navigate to the Runs tab in the Jobs UI to immediately review the processing notebook.
optionC: There is no way to determine why a Job task is running slowly.
optionD: They can navigate to the Tasks tab in the Jobs UI and click on the active run to review the processing notebook.
optionE: They can navigate to the Runs tab in the Jobs UI and click on the active run to review the processing notebook.
explanation:
Navigating to the Runs tab in the Jobs UI and clicking on the active run is how the tech lead reaches the slow notebook. Job run details live under Runs, and opening the run reaches the task's output, its Spark UI and its logs, which is what diagnosing a slow notebook requires.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Tasks tab, immediately) — the Tasks tab shows how the job is defined, not what any execution is doing, and stops short of opening a run.
Option B (Runs tab, immediately) — the right tab, but the notebook output is only visible after clicking into the run.
Option C (no way to determine) — false; the run view exists for exactly this.
Option D (Tasks tab, then click the active run) — the Tasks tab lists task definitions and dependencies; the run list is on the Runs tab.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/monitor

question: Which method should a Data Engineer apply to ensure Workflows are being triggered on schedule?
optionA: Scheduled Workflows can reduce resource consumption and expense since the cluster runs only long enough to execute the pipeline.
optionB: Scheduled Workflows run continuously until manually stopped.
optionC: Scheduled Workflows require an always-running cluster, which is more expensive but reduces processing latency.
optionD: Scheduled Workflows process data as it arrives at configured sources.
explanation:
Scheduled Workflows reduce resource consumption and expense because the cluster runs only long enough to execute the pipeline. Scheduling a workflow lets Databricks run it on job compute that is created for the run and terminated when it finishes, so the cluster exists only for as long as the pipeline takes, rather than being left available around the clock.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (run continuously until manually stopped) — a scheduled run starts at its trigger time and ends when the run completes.
Option C (require an always-running cluster) — that describes an all-purpose cluster left on; job compute is created per run.
Option D (process data as it arrives) — that is file-arrival or continuous triggering, a different trigger type from a schedule.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/triggers

question: A data engineer is getting a partner organization up to speed with Databricks account. Both teams share some business use cases. The data engineer has to share some of your Unity-Catalog managed delta tables and the notebook jobs creating those tables with the partner organization. How can the data engineer seamlessly share the required information?
optionA: Zip all the code and share via email and allow data ingestion from your data lake
optionB: Data and Notebooks can be shared simply using Unity Catalog.
optionC: Share required datasets and notebooks via Delta Sharing. Manage permissions via Unity Catalog.
optionD: Share access to codebase via Github and allow them to ingest datasets from your Datalake.
explanation:
Sharing the required datasets and notebooks via Delta Sharing, with permissions managed in Unity Catalog, is the seamless route. Delta Sharing is what moves the data across organisational boundaries, and Unity Catalog is what governs who may see it: the provider creates a share containing the required tables, and Databricks-to-Databricks sharing can carry notebook files alongside them, so the partner receives both the datasets and the notebooks that build them without either side copying anything.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (zip the code and email it, allow ingestion from the data lake) — shares code out of band and leaves the data access ungoverned and unaudited.
Option B (Unity Catalog alone) — the distractor worth taking seriously: Unity Catalog governs objects within a metastore but does not by itself hand data to a different organisation's account; sharing is the transport, Unity Catalog the permission model.
Option D (GitHub for code, ingest from the data lake) — shares the code but, again, opens the storage rather than governing access to the tables.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/opensharing/share-data-databricks

question: A data engineer and data analyst are working together on a data pipeline. The data engineer is working on the raw, bronze, and silver layers of the pipeline using Python, and the data analyst is working on the gold layer of the pipeline using SQL. The raw source of the pipeline is a streaming input. They now want to migrate their pipeline to use Delta Live Tables. Which change will need to be made to the pipeline when migrating to Delta Live Tables?
optionA: The pipeline can have different notebook sources in SQL & Python.
optionB: The pipeline will need to be written entirely in SQL.
optionC: The pipeline will need to be written entirely in Python.
optionD: The pipeline will need to use a batch source in place of a streaming source.
explanation:
The pipeline can have different notebook sources in SQL and Python, so no language change is needed. Delta Live Tables supports multi-language pipelines: a pipeline is configured with one or more source files, each in Python or SQL, and DLT resolves the dependencies between the datasets they declare. The engineer's Python bronze and silver layers and the analyst's SQL gold layer can be added as separate sources of the same pipeline.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (rewritten entirely in SQL) — unnecessary; Python sources are supported alongside SQL.
Option C (rewritten entirely in Python) — unnecessary for the same reason.
Option D (a batch source instead of streaming) — DLT streaming tables are built for streaming input; the source does not have to change.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/configure-pipeline

question: A data engineer has been using a Databricks SQL dashboard to monitor the cleanliness of the input data to an ELT job. The ELT job has its Databricks SQL query that returns the number of input records containing unexpected NULL values. The data engineer wants their entire team to be notified via a messaging webhook whenever this value reaches 100. Which of the following approaches can the data engineer use to notify their entire team via a messaging webhook whenever the number of NULL values reaches 100?
optionA: They can set up an Alert with a custom template.
optionB: They can set up an Alert with a new email alert destination.
optionC: They can set up an Alert with a new webhook alert destination.
optionD: They can set up an Alert with one-time notifications.
optionE: They can set up an Alert without notifications.
explanation:
Setting up an Alert with a new webhook alert destination is how the team gets notified over a messaging webhook. A webhook notification destination sends an HTTP request to an external endpoint when the alert fires — Slack, Microsoft Teams and similar integrations are built this way. The steps: create the webhook destination under notification destinations (admin settings), then open the query that counts unexpected NULLs, create an alert with the condition "value >= 100", and select the webhook destination in the alert's notification settings.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (an Alert with a custom template) — a template shapes the message body; it does not choose where the message is delivered.
Option B (a new email alert destination) — delivers by email, not through the messaging webhook the team asked for.
Option D (one-time notifications) — the team wants to hear whenever the value reaches 100, which needs the alert to keep evaluating and notifying.
Option E (an Alert without notifications) — an alert that notifies no one does not meet the requirement.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/user/alerts/

question: A data engineer needs to process SQL queries on a large dataset with fluctuating workloads. The workload requires automatic scaling based on the volume of queries, without the need to manage or provision infrastructure. The solution should be cost-efficient and charge only for the compute resources used during query execution. Which compute option should the data engineer use?
optionA: Databricks Jobs
optionB: Serverless SQL Warehouse
optionC: Databricks Runtime for ML
optionD: Databricks SQL Analytics
explanation:
A Serverless SQL Warehouse is the compute option. It starts in seconds, scales up and back down with query volume, and bills only for the time it spends executing, which matches every constraint in the question — fluctuating demand, no infrastructure to provision, and payment tied to actual use.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Databricks Jobs) — an orchestrator rather than a SQL query engine; it schedules work, it does not answer interactive SQL.
Option C (Databricks Runtime for ML) — a runtime image aimed at model training, not a compute type for SQL analytics.
Option D (Databricks SQL Analytics) — names the product surface rather than the compute option; any warehouse behind it would still have to be a serverless, pro or classic one.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/admin/sql/serverless

question: What is stored in a Databricks customer's cloud account?
optionA: Data
optionB: Cluster management metadata
optionC: Databricks web application
optionD: Notebooks
explanation:
Data is what is stored in the customer's cloud account. Databricks separates a control plane, which holds the backend services Databricks manages in its own account, from the compute plane and storage in the customer's account. The customer's cloud storage holds the tables and files the workspace works with (plus a workspace storage bucket for DBFS root and workspace system data such as logs and job run details); the control plane holds the web application, cluster management and the notebook service.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (cluster management metadata) — held and managed by Databricks in the control plane.
Option C (the Databricks web application) — a service Databricks runs in the control plane, not something in the customer's account.
Option D (notebooks) — notebook source is stored and served from the control plane; only revision and run data lands in the customer's workspace storage bucket, which is not what this option means.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/getting-started/overview

question: A data engineer is maintaining a data pipeline. Upon data ingestion, the data engineer notices that the source data is starting to have a lower level of quality. The data engineer would like to automate the process of monitoring the quality level. Which of the following tools can the data engineer use to solve this problem?
optionA: Unity Catalog
optionB: Auto Loader
optionC: Delta Live Tables
optionD: Delta Lake
optionE: Data Explorer
explanation:
Delta Live Tables is the tool for automating data-quality monitoring, through pipeline expectations. Declaring a constraint on a dataset makes each run evaluate incoming records against it and record how many passed and failed, so quality is tracked continuously as part of the pipeline instead of being spot-checked by hand — and the action attached to the constraint decides whether violating rows are kept, dropped or made to fail the update.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Unity Catalog) — governs access and lineage; it does not evaluate record quality.
Option B (Auto Loader) — ingests new files but does not judge their contents.
Option D (Delta Lake) — enforces schema and gives ACID guarantees, which stops malformed writes but does not measure quality over time.
Option E (Data Explorer) — Catalog Explorer under its former name; a browsing UI, not a monitoring mechanism.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectations

question: What are the transformations typically included in building the Bronze layer?
optionA: Include columns Load date/time, process ID
optionB: Business rules and transformations
optionC: Perform extensive data cleansing
optionD: Aggregate data from multiple sources
explanation:
Including columns such as load date/time and process ID is the transformation that belongs in the Bronze layer. Bronze stores source data essentially as it arrived, so the only additions belonging there are the ones that record provenance rather than change meaning: load timestamp, a process or batch id, source file name. Those columns are what make a load auditable and reprocessable later.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (business rules and transformations) — Silver-to-Gold work; applying them at Bronze loses the record of what the source actually sent.
Option C (extensive data cleansing) — Silver's job; Bronze keeps the raw shape.
Option D (aggregate data from multiple sources) — characteristic of Gold, the consumption layer.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

question: A data engineer is decommissioning a sandbox schema in Unity Catalog. Some tables are ephemeral staging outputs that can be safety removed entirely, but a few tables point at shared cloud storage used by downstream jobs outside Databricks. The engineer must avoid deleting any shared files when cleaning up catalog objects. How does Unity Catalog behave when dropping Managed vs External tables?
optionA: DROP all tables; Databricks will only remove metadata for both managed and external tables.
optionB: DROP managed tables that are ephemeral and DROP external tables; files for both remain for 7 days.
optionC: DROP managed staging tables to remove data and metadata, and DROP external tables to remove only metadata
optionD: DROP external tables first to delete their files, then DROP managed tables to keep their files for recovery.
explanation:
Dropping managed staging tables removes data and metadata, and dropping external tables removes only metadata — which is exactly the split the engineer needs. In Unity Catalog a managed table's files live in storage Databricks controls, so DROP deletes both the catalog entry and the underlying files; an external table points at a location the customer controls, so DROP removes the catalog entry and leaves the shared files intact for the downstream jobs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (only metadata removed for both) — wrong for managed tables, whose data files are deleted with the table.
Option B (files for both remain for 7 days) — managed-table data is deleted on drop (Unity Catalog retains it briefly for UNDROP, but that is not a 7-day file retention for both kinds); external files are never touched at all.
Option D (drop external tables first to delete their files) — backwards: dropping an external table never deletes its files.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/external
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/managed

question: A data engineer is writing Spark code to group sales data by region and calculate total revenue for each region. Which Spark DataFrame transformation performs grouping operations?
optionA: orderBy
optionB: groupBy
optionC: filter
optionD: select
explanation:
groupBy is the grouping transformation. It partitions rows by the values of the given column and returns a grouped object that an aggregation such as sum then reduces, producing one row per region.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (orderBy) — sorts rows; it does not collapse them.
Option C (filter) — removes rows that fail a predicate.
Option D (select) — projects a subset of columns. Any of these can appear in the same pipeline, but none turns many rows per region into one.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-groupby

question: A data engineer has realized that they made a mistake when making a daily update to a table. They need to use Delta time travel to restore the table to a version that is 3 days old. However, when the data engineer attempts to time travel to the older version, they are unable to restore the data because the data files have been deleted. Which of the following explains why the data files are no longer present?
optionA: The VACUUM command was run on the table
optionB: The TIME TRAVEL command was run on the table
optionC: The DELETE HISTORY command was run on the table
optionD: The OPTIMIZE command was nun on the table
optionE: The HISTORY command was run on the table
explanation:
The VACUUM command was run on the table. VACUUM removes data files no longer referenced by the current table version and older than the retention threshold (7 days by default), and those files are what time travel needs to reconstruct an earlier version. Once VACUUM has removed the files behind the 3-day-old version, RESTORE and SELECT ... VERSION AS OF can no longer read it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (TIME TRAVEL command) — there is no such command; time travel is a query clause (VERSION AS OF, TIMESTAMP AS OF) and reads files rather than deleting them.
Option C (DELETE HISTORY command) — not a Delta command.
Option D (OPTIMIZE) — compacts small files into larger ones but leaves the old files in place for time travel until VACUUM removes them.
Option E (HISTORY command) — DESCRIBE HISTORY only lists the table's versions; it deletes nothing.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/operations/vacuum
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/history

question: A data engineer has configured a Structured Streaming job to read from a table, manipulate the data, and then perform a streaming write into a new table. The code block used by the data engineer is below: If the data engineer only wants the query to execute a micro-batch to process data every 5 seconds, which of the following lines of code should the data engineer use to fill in the blank?
optionA: trigger(continuous="5 seconds")
optionB: trigger("5 seconds")
optionC: trigger(processingTime="5 seconds")
optionD: trigger(once="5 seconds")
optionE: trigger()
explanation:
trigger(processingTime="5 seconds") sets a fixed micro-batch interval, which is exactly what the question describes — run a micro-batch, wait until five seconds have elapsed, run the next.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (trigger(continuous="5 seconds")) — selects continuous processing, an experimental Spark mode Databricks does not support, and the interval there is a checkpointing interval rather than a batch interval.
Option B (trigger("5 seconds")) — not a valid call; the mode has to be named with a keyword argument.
Option D (trigger(once="5 seconds")) — once takes a boolean and runs a single batch, not a repeating one.
Option E (trigger()) — no arguments is not a valid call either.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/structured-streaming/triggers

question: In which of the following scenarios should a data engineer select a Task in the Depends On field of a new Databricks Job Task?
optionA: When another task needs to fail before the new task begins
optionB: When another task needs to be replaced by the new task
optionC: When another task needs to use as little compute resources as possible
optionD: When another task has the same dependency libraries as the new task
optionE: When another task needs to successfully complete before the new task begins
explanation:
When another task needs to successfully complete before the new task begins is the scenario for the Depends on field. It expresses task ordering: the new task waits until the named task has finished successfully before it starts, which is what lets a job express a pipeline rather than a set of unrelated tasks.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (another task needs to fail first) — a dependency that fails leaves the dependent task unrun rather than starting it; a run-on-failure condition is a separate "Run if" setting.
Option B (another task needs to be replaced) — Depends on does not replace anything.
Option C (another task should use as little compute as possible) — ordering has no effect on how much compute a task uses.
Option D (another task shares dependency libraries) — libraries are configured per task independently of ordering.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/configure-task

question: A data engineer needs to apply custom logic to identify employees with more than 5 years of experience in array column employees in table stores. The custom logic should create a new column exp_employees that is an array of all of the employees with more than 5 years of experience for each row. In order to apply this custom logic at scale, the data engineer wants to use the FILTER higher-order function. Which of the following code blocks successfully completes this task?
optionA:
```sql
SELECT
    store_id,
    employees,
    FILTER (employees, years_exp > 5) AS exp_employees
FROM stores;
```
optionB:
```sql
SELECT
    store_id,
    employees,
    CASE WHEN employees.years_exp > 5 THEN employees
        ELSE NULL
    END AS exp_employees
FROM stores;
```
optionC:
```sql
SELECT
    store_id,
    employees,
    FILTER (employees, i -> i.years_exp > 5) AS exp_employees
FROM stores;
```
optionD:
```sql
SELECT
    store_id,
    employees,
    FILTER (exp_employees, i -> i.years_exp > 5) AS exp_employees
FROM stores;
```
optionE:
```sql
SELECT
    store_id,
    employees,
    FILTER (exp_employees, years_exp > 5) AS exp_employees
FROM stores;
```
explanation:
FILTER (employees, i -> i.years_exp > 5) AS exp_employees is the block that works. FILTER is a higher-order function, so its second argument has to be a lambda that names the element being tested; the lambda runs per element of the array and keeps the ones satisfying the predicate, producing a new array per row — which is what the question asks for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (FILTER (employees, years_exp > 5)) — drops the lambda, so years_exp has no element to bind to and does not resolve.
Option B (CASE WHEN employees.years_exp > 5) — tests employees.years_exp as though the column were a struct, and returns the whole array or NULL rather than filtering element by element.
Option D (FILTER (exp_employees, i -> ...)) — filters exp_employees, the column being created, rather than employees, the column that exists.
Option E (FILTER (exp_employees, years_exp > 5)) — both mistakes at once: the wrong column and no lambda.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/functions/filter

question: A Databricks workflow fails at the last stage due to an error in a notebook. This workflow runs daily. The data engineer fixes the mistake and wants to rerun the pipeline. This workflow is very costly and time-intensive to run. Which action should the data engineer do in order to minimise downtime and cost?
optionA: Re-run the entire workflow
optionB: Repair run
optionC: Restart the cluster
optionD: Switch to another cluster
explanation:
Repair run is the action. It re-executes only the tasks that failed, together with anything downstream that never got to run, and reuses the successful output of everything before them. On an expensive, long pipeline whose last stage broke, that is the difference between rerunning one task and rerunning the whole thing.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (re-run the entire workflow) — produces the right result but repeats hours of work that already succeeded, exactly the cost the question asks to avoid.
Option C (restart the cluster) — addresses compute, and the failure came from a mistake in the notebook; new compute runs the same broken code.
Option D (switch to another cluster) — the same problem, plus a reconfiguration step.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/repair-job-failures

question: A data engineer is designing a streaming pipeline and wants to limit how long Spark maintains state information for aggregation queries. Which Structured Streaming feature defines how long late data can be processed?
optionA: Watermark
optionB: Cache
optionC: Checkpoint
optionD: Partition
explanation:
A watermark is the Structured Streaming feature that defines how long late data can be processed. It declares how late an event may arrive and still be counted, which lets Spark decide when a window can be finalised and its state discarded — so it answers both halves of the question, how long late data is accepted and how long state is retained.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Cache) — keeps data in memory for reuse; nothing to do with event-time lateness.
Option C (Checkpoint) — the closest distractor, and it does something different: it records stream progress so a query can restart without reprocessing or losing data. It persists state rather than bounding it.
Option D (Partition) — controls data layout, not state lifetime.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/structured-streaming/watermarks

question: An engineering manager uses a Databricks SQL query to monitor ingestion latency for each data source. The manager checks the results of the query every day, but they are manually rerunning the query each day and waiting for the results. Which of the following approaches can the manager use to ensure the results of the query are updated each day?
optionA: They can schedule the query to refresh every 1 day from the SQL endpoint's page in Databricks SQL.
optionB: They can schedule the query to refresh every 1 day from the query's page in Databricks SQL.
optionC: They can schedule the query to run every 1 day from the Jobs UI.
optionD: They can schedule the query to refresh every 12 hours from the SQL endpoint's page in Databricks SQL.
optionE: They can schedule the query to run every 12 hours from the Jobs UI.
explanation:
Scheduling the query to refresh every 1 day from the query's page in Databricks SQL is the approach. A Databricks SQL query is scheduled from its own page: opening the query and setting a refresh schedule there makes it re-run on that cadence and update its results, and anything reading those results, such as a dashboard, picks up the refreshed output.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (every 1 day from the SQL endpoint's page) — a warehouse is compute with settings for size, scaling and auto-stop; schedules belong to queries, not to the warehouse that runs them.
Option C (every 1 day from the Jobs UI) — a job could run a SQL task, but the question is about refreshing a Databricks SQL query's results, which the query's own schedule does directly.
Option D (every 12 hours from the SQL endpoint's page) — wrong place, and twice the cadence asked for.
Option E (every 12 hours from the Jobs UI) — the manager checks once a day; a twelve-hour schedule answers a different question.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/user/queries/schedule-query

question:
A dataset has been defined using Delta Live Tables and includes an expectations clause:
```sql
CONSTRAINT valid_timestamp EXPECT (timestamp > '2020-01-01') ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE
```
What is the expected behavior when a batch of data containing data that violates these constraints is processed?
optionA: Records that violate the expectation are added to the target dataset and recorded as invalid in the event log.
optionB: Records that violate the expectation are added to the target dataset and flagged as invalid in a field added to the target dataset.
optionC: Records that violate the expectation are dropped from the target dataset and recorded as invalid in the event log.
optionD: Records that violate the expectation are dropped from the target dataset and loaded into a quarantine table.
optionE: Records that violate the expectation cause the job to fail.
explanation:
Records that violate the expectation cause the job to fail. The constraint here carries ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE, and that action stops the pipeline: Databricks documents it as invalid records preventing the update from succeeding, with manual intervention required before reprocessing — so a batch containing a timestamp at or before 2020-01-01 fails the run outright.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (added to the target and recorded as invalid in the event log) — the default warn behaviour of a bare EXPECT with no ON VIOLATION clause.
Option B (added to the target and flagged in an added field) — no expectation action adds a column to the target dataset.
Option C (dropped and recorded in the event log) — that is ON VIOLATION DROP ROW, not the action in this clause.
Option D (dropped and loaded into a quarantine table) — a pattern you build yourself with additional datasets; no ON VIOLATION action does it for you.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectations

question: A data engineer is attempting to drop a Spark SQL table my_table and runs the following command: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS my_table; After running this command, the engineer notices that the data files and metadata files have been deleted from the file system. Which of the following describes why all of these files were deleted?
optionA: The table was managed
optionB: The table did not have a location
optionC: The table's data was larger than 10 GB
optionD: The table's data was smaller than 10 GB
optionE: The table was external
explanation:
The table was managed. Dropping a managed table removes its data as well as its metadata, because Databricks owns the storage for managed tables and treats the table definition and the files beneath it as one lifecycle.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (the table did not have a location) — a table created without a LOCATION is simply a managed table, so this restates the answer indirectly rather than explaining the deletion.
Option C (data larger than 10 GB) — invented; nothing about DROP TABLE depends on the size of the data.
Option D (data smaller than 10 GB) — invented for the same reason.
Option E (the table was external) — the opposite behaviour: dropping an external table removes the catalog entry and leaves the files untouched.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/managed

question: Which of the following data workloads will utilize a Gold table as its source?
optionA: A job that cleans data by removing malformatted records
optionB: A job that queries aggregated data designed to feed into a dashboard
optionC: A job that aggregates uncleaned data to create standard summary statistics
optionD: A job that ingests raw data from a streaming source into the Lakehouse
optionE: A job that enriches data by parsing its timestamps into a human-readable format
explanation:
A job that queries aggregated data designed to feed into a dashboard is the workload that reads from a Gold table. Gold tables are the refined, aggregated end of the medallion architecture, so the workload that reads from them is the one already consuming business-ready output.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (cleans data by removing malformatted records) — a Bronze-to-Silver step; it reads raw data.
Option C (aggregates uncleaned data into summary statistics) — the giveaway is "uncleaned": its source has not been through Silver yet, so it is not Gold no matter that its output is aggregated.
Option D (ingests raw streaming data into the Lakehouse) — lands in Bronze; its source is outside the lakehouse entirely.
Option E (parses timestamps into a readable format) — enrichment on the way to Silver, reading Bronze.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

question: Differentiate between all-purpose clusters and jobs clusters. A data engineering team has created a python notebook to load data from cloud storage, this job has been tested and now needs to be scheduled in production. Which would be the best cluster to be used in this case?
optionA: Any Unity Catalog-enabled cluster
optionB: All purpose cluster
optionC: Jobs Cluster
optionD: Serverless SQL warehouse
explanation:
A jobs cluster is the right compute for scheduled production work. It is created when the run starts, sized by the job's configuration, and terminated when the run ends, so nothing is paid for between nightly runs and each run gets a clean, predictable environment.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (any Unity Catalog-enabled cluster) — describes a governance property rather than a cluster type, so it does not answer the question.
Option B (all-purpose cluster) — designed for interactive development, stays available between uses and is billed at a higher rate; the expensive choice for scheduled work.
Option D (serverless SQL warehouse) — runs SQL, not a Python notebook.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/compute

question: A data engineer needs to develop integration tests for an ETL process and deploy a version- controlled, packaged workflow into production using an external job scheduler. Which tool should the data engineer use for this job?
optionA: Databricks Connect
optionB: Databricks Asset Bundles
optionC: Databricks Command Line Interface
optionD: Databricks Software Development Kit
explanation:
Databricks Asset Bundles are the tool. Bundles package a project's jobs, pipelines and settings as YAML that lives in the repository beside the code, which makes the workflow version-controlled and reviewable, gives integration tests a defined target to deploy against, and produces a deployment an external scheduler can invoke through the CLI.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Databricks Connect) — runs local code against a remote cluster, useful while developing but not a deployment mechanism.
Option C (Databricks CLI) — the closest answer: it is what bundles are deployed with, but it does not itself provide the versioned packaging.
Option D (Databricks SDK) — a programmatic client for the REST API, not a packaging format.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/bundles/

question: A data engineer has a Delta table containing old data files that are no longer referenced after several update and delete operations. To remove these unused files and reclaim storage space, which Delta Lake command should be executed?
optionA: OPTIMIZE
optionB: VACUUM
optionC: DESCRIBE HISTORY
optionD: CACHE TABLE
explanation:
VACUUM is the command that deletes files. Updates and deletes on a Delta table write new files and leave the superseded ones in place so time travel keeps working; VACUUM removes those unreferenced files once they are older than the retention threshold, which is what reclaims the storage. One consequence worth remembering: because VACUUM removes the files older versions depend on, running it also limits how far back time travel can reach.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (OPTIMIZE) — the closest distractor, and it does something different: it compacts many small files into fewer large ones to speed up reads, without removing history.
Option C (DESCRIBE HISTORY) — only reports the table's version log.
Option D (CACHE TABLE) — loads data into memory for faster access and changes nothing on disk.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/operations/vacuum

question: A global retail company sells products across multiple categories (e.g., Electronics, Clothing) and regions (e.g., North, South, East, West). The sales team has provided the data engineer with a PySpark dataframe named sales_df as below and the team wants the data engineer to analyze the sales data to help them make strategic decisions. Calculate the total sales amount for each product category and store the results in a new dataframe called category_sales. What will generate the expected result of category_sales?
optionA: category_sales = sales_df.groupBy("category").agg(sum("sales_amount").alias("total_sales_amount"))
optionB: category_sales = sales_df.sum("sales_amount").groupBy("category").alias("total_sales_amount"))
optionC: category_sales = sales_df.agg(sum("sales_amount").groupBy("category").alias("total_sales_amount"))
optionD: category_sales = sales_df.groupBy("region").agg(sum("sales_amount").alias("total_sales_amount"))
explanation:
category_sales = sales_df.groupBy("category").agg(sum("sales_amount").alias("total_sales_amount")) generates the expected result: group by the product category, then aggregate the sum of sales_amount, aliasing it as total_sales_amount. On the sample data that gives 500 for Electronics and 900 for Clothing.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (.sum("sales_amount").groupBy("category")) — calls .sum() before .groupBy(), collapsing the whole DataFrame to one row first and leaving nothing to group.
Option C (.agg(sum(...).groupBy("category"))) — nests .groupBy() inside .agg(), which is not valid; grouping must come before aggregation.
Option D (.groupBy("region")) — correct structure but the wrong key; it totals by region, not by product category.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-groupby

question: Which of the following code blocks will remove the rows where the value in column age is greater than 25 from the existing Delta table my_table and save the updated table?
optionA: UPDATE my_table WHERE age <= 25;
optionB: UPDATE my_table WHERE age > 25;
optionC: DELETE FROM my_table WHERE age <= 25;
optionD: SELECT * FROM my_table WHERE age > 25;
optionE: DELETE FROM my_table WHERE age > 25;
explanation:
DELETE FROM my_table WHERE age > 25; removes the rows the question describes and, because Delta tables are transactional, the change is committed to the table itself — there is no separate save step.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (UPDATE my_table WHERE age <= 25) — UPDATE modifies rows rather than removing them, carries no SET clause as written, and targets the wrong rows.
Option B (UPDATE my_table WHERE age > 25) — the right predicate but still an UPDATE with no SET clause; nothing is removed.
Option C (DELETE FROM my_table WHERE age <= 25) — deletes precisely the rows meant to be kept.
Option D (SELECT * FROM my_table WHERE age > 25) — only reads, returning the matching rows and leaving the table untouched.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/delta-delete-from

question: A data architect has determined that a table of the following format is necessary: Which of the following code blocks uses SQL DDL commands to create an empty Delta table in the above format regardless of whether a table already exists with this name?
optionA:
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE table_name (
  employeeId STRING,
  startDate DATE,
  avgRating FLOAT
)
```
optionB:
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE table_name WITH COLUMNS (
  employeeId STRING,
  startDate DATE,
  avgRating FLOAT
) USING DELTA
```
optionC:
```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS table_name (
  employeeId STRING,
  startDate DATE,
  avgRating FLOAT
)
```
optionD:
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE table_name AS
SELECT
  employeeId STRING,
  startDate DATE,
  avgRating FLOAT
USING DELTA
```
optionE:
```sql
CREATE TABLE table_name AS
SELECT
  employeeId STRING,
  startDate DATE,
  avgRating FLOAT
```
explanation:
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE table_name (employeeId STRING, startDate DATE, avgRating FLOAT) is the block. CREATE OR REPLACE creates the table when it is absent and overwrites the definition when it is present, which is what "regardless of whether a table already exists" asks for. Listing the columns and their types produces the empty table in the required shape, and Delta is the default format so no USING clause is needed.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... WITH COLUMNS) — WITH COLUMNS is not valid syntax.
Option C (CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS) — the trap: it succeeds either way, but when a table of that name already exists it silently leaves the old definition in place, so the schema may not be the one required.
Option D (CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT ... USING DELTA) — AS SELECT builds a table from query results, and a SELECT list cannot carry column type declarations.
Option E (CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT) — the same structural problem, and no OR REPLACE, so it fails if the table exists.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-create-table-using

question: A data engineer team has decided to implement a new data platform on Databricks and is currently deciding how to store each kind of data on each data layer. What is the appropriate layer and data pairing for medallion architecture?
optionA: Silver Layer - Raw data from deposit account application
optionB: Bronze Layer - Summary of cash deposit amount for each country and city
optionC: Silver Layer - Cleansed master customer data
optionD: Gold Layer - Deduplicated money transfer transaction
explanation:
Silver Layer paired with cleansed master customer data is the correct pairing. In the medallion architecture the Silver layer holds cleansed and conformed data — cleaned, validated and standardised after ingestion from Bronze — and master customer data is the textbook example.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Silver — raw data from a deposit account application) — raw source data belongs in Bronze.
Option B (Bronze — summary of cash deposits per country and city) — an aggregate, which is Gold-layer output, not raw landing data.
Option D (Gold — deduplicated money transfer transactions) — deduplicated transactional records are Silver; Gold holds the business-level aggregates built from them.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

question: A data engineer must deliver a trustworthy customer 360 dataset in Databricks for data scientists and BI teams. The engineer plans to join deduplicated customer records with cleaned transaction data, enforce schema and data quality checks, and create a conformed "customer_transactions"view. Later, highly aggregated, domain-specific tables (for weekly spend and executive summaries) will be produced for dashboards. Where should the engineer build the conformed "customer_transactions" dataset, and where should the aggregated, report-ready tables reside?
optionA: Build both "customer_transactions" and aggregated, report-ready tables in Silver to keep the model simpler.
optionB: Build "customer_transactions" in Bronze and put the aggregated, report-ready tables in Silver.
optionC: Build "customer_transactions" in Gold and put the aggregated, report-ready tables in Silver.
optionD: Build "customer_transactions" in Silver and put the aggregated, report-ready tables in Gold.
explanation:
Building customer_transactions in Silver and the aggregated, report-ready tables in Gold is the right placement. The conformed dataset represents cleaned, deduplicated and validated data suitable for broad analytical use, which is Silver's role; the aggregated, domain-specific tables for dashboards and executive reporting are what Gold is designed for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (both in Silver) — puts consumption-ready aggregates in the conformed layer, losing the separation the architecture is built on.
Option B (customer_transactions in Bronze, aggregates in Silver) — Bronze is raw landing data, not a joined and validated view; everything is one layer too early.
Option C (customer_transactions in Gold, aggregates in Silver) — backwards: the conformed dataset feeds the aggregates, so it must sit upstream of them.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

question: A data engineer needs to apply custom logic to string column city in table stores for a specific use case. In order to apply this custom logic at scale, the data engineer wants to create a SQL user- defined function (UDF). Which of the following code blocks creates this SQL UDF?
optionA:
```sql
CREATE UDF combine_nyc(city STRING)
RETURN CASE
  WHEN city = "brooklyn" THEN "new york"
  ELSE city
END;
```
optionB:
```sql
CREATE UDF combine_nyc(city STRING)
RETURNS STRING
CASE
  WHEN city = "brooklyn" THEN "new york"
  ELSE city
END;
```
optionC:
```sql
CREATE UDF combine_nyc(city STRING)
RETURNS STRING
RETURN CASE
  WHEN city = "brooklyn" THEN "new york"
  ELSE city
END;
```
optionD:
```sql
CREATE FUNCTION combine_nyc(city STRING)
RETURN CASE
  WHEN city = "brooklyn" THEN "new york"
  ELSE city
END;
```
optionE:
```sql
CREATE FUNCTION combine_nyc(city STRING)
RETURNS STRING
RETURN CASE
  WHEN city = "brooklyn" THEN "new york"
  ELSE city
END;
```
explanation:
CREATE FUNCTION combine_nyc(city STRING) RETURNS STRING RETURN CASE ... END; is the block that creates the SQL UDF. A SQL UDF is created with CREATE FUNCTION, must declare its return type with RETURNS, and must produce its value with RETURN, and only this option has all three.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (CREATE UDF ... RETURN CASE) — CREATE UDF is not a keyword in Databricks SQL, and the return type is missing.
Option B (CREATE UDF ... RETURNS STRING CASE) — wrong keyword, and the body starts with CASE instead of RETURN CASE, so there is no return statement.
Option C (CREATE UDF ... RETURNS STRING RETURN CASE) — the right shape with the wrong keyword; CREATE UDF does not parse.
Option D (CREATE FUNCTION ... RETURN CASE) — omits RETURNS STRING, so the function has no declared type.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-create-sql-function

question: An organization has data stored across multiple external systems, including MySQL, Amazon Redshift, and Google BigQuery. The data engineer wants to perform analytics without ingesting directly into Databricks, ensuring unified governance and minimizing data duplication. Which feature of Databricks enables querying these external data sources while maintaining centralized governance?
optionA: Delta Lake
optionB: Lakehouse Federation
optionC: MLflow
optionD: Databricks Connect
explanation:
Lakehouse Federation is the feature that queries MySQL, Redshift and BigQuery without ingesting them. A connection and a foreign catalog are registered for each source, their tables become queryable through Unity Catalog, and access is governed centrally there — so there is no copy to keep in sync and no duplication.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Delta Lake) — the storage format for tables inside the lakehouse; it does not reach external databases.
Option C (MLflow) — the machine-learning lifecycle tool; nothing to do with querying external sources.
Option D (Databricks Connect) — runs local IDE code against a remote cluster; it is a developer tool, not a federation layer.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/query-federation/

question:
A dataset has been defined using Delta Live Tables and includes an expectations clause:
```sql
CONSTRAINT valid_timestamp EXPECT (timestamp > '2020-01-01') ON VIOLATION DROP ROW
```
What is the expected behavior when a batch of data containing data that violates these constraints is processed?
optionA: Records that violate the expectation are added to the target dataset and flagged as invalid in a field added to the target dataset.
optionB: Records that violate the expectation are dropped from the target dataset and loaded into a quarantine table.
optionC: Records that violate the expectation are dropped from the target dataset and recorded as invalid in the event log.
optionD: Records that violate the expectation are added to the target dataset and recorded as invalid in the event log.
optionE: Records that violate the expectation cause the job to fail.
explanation:
Records that violate the expectation are dropped from the target dataset and recorded as invalid in the event log. This constraint carries ON VIOLATION DROP ROW, so violating records never reach the target; Databricks documents that action as dropping invalid records before the data is written, with the count of dropped records logged alongside the dataset's other metrics in the event log.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (added to the target and flagged in an added field) — no expectation action adds a validity column to the target.
Option B (dropped and loaded into a quarantine table) — a pattern you build with extra datasets rather than something an ON VIOLATION action does.
Option D (added to the target and recorded in the event log) — the default warn behaviour of a bare EXPECT with no ON VIOLATION clause.
Option E (cause the job to fail) — that is ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE, not the action in this clause.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectations

question: A Data Engineer is designing Bronze layer in Databricks Medallion Architecture. The raw data is collected from multiple sources (Clickstream in JSON, Transactions in CSV). The task is to design the Bronze layer of the Medallion Architecture to ingest and store this raw data for further processing. Which operation applies to the Bronze layer?
optionA: Ingest raw data without transformations, preserving original schemas, and store in Delta format.
optionB: Clean and standardize raw data by removing null values and enforcing schemas.
optionC: Apply complex business logic to enrich raw data with customer segmentation labels.
optionD: Aggregate and transform source data to calculate daily sales performance metrics.
explanation:
Ingesting raw data without transformations, preserving original schemas, and storing it in Delta format is the Bronze-layer operation. Bronze lands raw data from every source as it arrived — the JSON clickstream and the CSV transactions alike — in Delta so it is durable and queryable, serving as the source of truth for the Silver and Gold layers where cleaning, standardisation and business logic are applied.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (clean and standardise, remove nulls, enforce schemas) — Silver's job; doing it at Bronze loses the record of what the source actually sent.
Option C (enrich with customer segmentation labels) — business logic, applied in Silver or Gold.
Option D (aggregate into daily sales metrics) — Gold-layer output.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

question: A data engineer has configured a Structured Streaming job to read from a table, manipulate the data, and then perform a streaming write into a new table. The code block used by the data engineer is below: The data engineer only wants the query to process all of the available data in as many batches as required. Which line of code should the data engineer use to fill in the blank?
optionA: trigger(continuous="once")
optionB: trigger(processingTime="once")
optionC: trigger(availableNow=True)
optionD: trigger(once=True)
explanation:
trigger(availableNow=True) is the line that processes everything currently available and then stops. Databricks describes it as consuming all available records as an incremental batch, with the batch size configurable through options such as maxBytesPerTrigger, which is exactly the "as many batches as required" behaviour the question asks for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (trigger(continuous="once")) — continuous processing is an unsupported experimental Spark feature, and its argument is a checkpoint interval, not "once".
Option B (trigger(processingTime="once")) — processingTime takes an interval and runs on it indefinitely; "once" is not an interval.
Option D (trigger(once=True)) — the near-miss: it also processes all available data and stops, but as a single batch, which can overwhelm a cluster with a large backlog. It is also deprecated — Databricks states that in Databricks Runtime 11.3 LTS and above, Trigger.Once is deprecated and recommends Trigger.AvailableNow for all incremental batch processing workloads.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/structured-streaming/triggers

corrected.note: Answer stands. Added the specific distinction the item turns on -- AvailableNow splits the backlog into multiple incremental batches while Once uses a single batch -- and recorded that Trigger.Once has been deprecated since Databricks Runtime 11.3 LTS.

question: Which of the following commands will return the number of null values in the member_id column?
optionA: SELECT count(member_id) - count_null(member_id) FROM my_table;
optionB: SELECT null(member_id) FROM my_table;
optionC: SELECT count_if(member_id IS NULL) FROM my_table;
optionD: SELECT count(member_id) FROM my_table;
optionE: SELECT count_null(member_id) FROM my_table;
explanation:
SELECT count_if(member_id IS NULL) FROM my_table; counts the rows where the predicate holds, so it returns the number of nulls directly. The IS NULL test matters: a comparison such as member_id = NULL would evaluate to NULL for every row and count nothing. A useful equivalent, if you want to remember only one form, is count(*) - count(member_id).
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (count(member_id) - count_null(member_id)) — count_null does not exist in Databricks SQL, and the arithmetic would be wrong even if it did.
Option B (null(member_id)) — not a function.
Option D (count(member_id)) — counts the non-null values, the opposite of what is asked.
Option E (count_null(member_id)) — no such function.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/functions/count_if

question: What Databricks feature can be used to check the data sources and tables used in a workspace?
optionA: Use the lineage feature to visualize a graph that highlights where the table is used only in reports.
optionB: Use the lineage feature to visualize a graph that highlights where the table is used only in notebooks.
optionC: Use the lineage feature to visualize a graph that shows all dependencies, including where the table is used in notebooks, other tables, and reports.
optionD: Do not use the lineage feature as it only tracks activity from the last 3 months and will not provide full details on dependencies.
explanation:
Using the lineage feature to visualise a graph that shows all dependencies — where the table is used in notebooks, other tables and reports — is the answer. Unity Catalog captures lineage automatically for queries run on Databricks, down to the column level, and aggregates it across every workspace attached to the metastore. The documentation describes it as showing which queries and files populate a table, which jobs and notebooks transform it, and which dashboards consume the results.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (lineage limited to reports) — the graph is not limited to any one consumer type.
Option B (lineage limited to notebooks) — the same; notebooks are one node type among several.
Option D (do not use lineage, three-month retention) — lineage data displayed in Catalog Explorer is retained indefinitely, with all lineage captured after September 1, 2024 available; there is no three-month window.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/data-lineage

question: A data engineer is implementing a data ingestion pipeline that automatically detects schema changes in incoming JSON files and evolves the target Delta table accordingly. Which feature supports this automatic schema evolution?
optionA: Broadcast join
optionB: Partition pruning
optionC: Schema evolution
optionD: Schema enforcement
explanation:
Schema evolution is the feature that lets the target table's schema change as incoming data changes. In an Auto Loader pipeline it is controlled by cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode, whose default adds newly discovered columns to the schema; on the write side, the mergeSchema option lets a Delta write add new columns rather than reject them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (broadcast join) — a query optimisation for joining a small table; nothing to do with schema.
Option B (partition pruning) — a read optimisation that skips partitions; nothing to do with schema.
Option D (schema enforcement) — the deliberate opposite and the tempting distractor: it rejects writes that do not match the current schema, protecting a table from unexpected columns rather than absorbing them. Enforcement is the default guard, evolution the explicit opt-in.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ingestion/cloud-object-storage/auto-loader/schema
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/update-schema

question: A data engineer is setting up a new Databricks pipeline that ingests clickstream events from Kafka and daily product catalogs from cloud object storage. To ensure auditability and easy reprocessing, the engineer wants to land all source data. Later stages will handle cleaning, deduplication, and business modeling before the data is used in dashboards. Which approach aligns to Medallion Architecture principles?
optionA: Land both sources in Gold with denormalized star schemas to optimize BI while retaining full source fidelity.
optionB: Land streaming events from Kafka in silver, and the product catalog directly in Gold to minimize layers for batch data.
optionC: Land both sources in the Bronze layer append-only with minimal validation, then build Silver/Gold downstream for quality and analytics.
optionD: Land both sources directly into the Silver layer with schema enforcement and deduplication to reduce downstream complexity.
explanation:
Landing both sources in the Bronze layer append-only with minimal validation, then building Silver and Gold downstream, is the approach aligned to the medallion architecture. Bronze preserves source fidelity for auditability and reprocessing; cleaning, deduplication and business modelling belong to Silver and Gold, which is where the question says they will happen.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (both in Gold as star schemas) — Gold is the curated end of the pipeline; landing raw data there skips the layers that make it trustworthy, and a star schema is not "full source fidelity".
Option B (Kafka to Silver, catalog to Gold) — neither source has been cleaned yet, and splitting them by layer breaks the uniform landing zone that reprocessing depends on.
Option D (both into Silver with enforcement and deduplication) — deduplication at landing discards raw records the engineer wants to keep for audit; Bronze exists so that nothing is lost on the way in.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

question: A data engineer wants to run SQL queries directly on data stored in Delta Lake using a serverless compute environment designed for analytics workloads. Which Databricks component provides this capability?
optionA: Spark Driver
optionB: DBFS
optionC: Databricks SQL Warehouse
optionD: MLflow
explanation:
A Databricks SQL Warehouse is the component that runs SQL directly against Delta Lake, and in its serverless form it starts in seconds, scales with demand and needs no infrastructure management — which matches every part of the question.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Spark Driver) — a component inside a cluster that coordinates work; it is not something you point SQL at.
Option B (DBFS) — a filesystem abstraction over object storage, not compute.
Option D (MLflow) — tracks experiments and manages models.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/sql-warehouse/

question: A data engineer has a Python notebook in Databricks, but they need to use SQL to accomplish a specific task within a cell. They still want all of the other cells to use Python without making any changes to those cells. Which of the following describes how the data engineer can use SQL within a cell of their Python notebook?
optionA: They can simply write SQL syntax in the cell
optionB: They can attach the cell to a SQL endpoint rather than a Databricks cluster
optionC: It is not possible to use SQL in a Python notebook
optionD: They can change the default language of the notebook to SQL
optionE: They can add %sql to the first line of the cell
explanation:
Adding %sql to the first line of the cell switches that one cell to SQL while every other cell keeps the notebook's default language. That is precisely the requirement — one cell changed, the rest untouched.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (simply write SQL syntax in the cell) — the cell is still interpreted as Python, so bare SQL fails.
Option B (attach the cell to a SQL endpoint) — cells attach to the notebook's compute; there is no per-cell warehouse attachment.
Option C (not possible) — false; language magics exist for exactly this.
Option D (change the notebook's default language to SQL) — flips every cell, which the question rules out.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/notebooks/notebooks-code

question: A data engineer wants to delete records from a Delta table where the status column equals "inactive". The operation should modify only the affected rows without rewriting the entire dataset. Which SQL command should be used?
optionA: DELETE
optionB: INSERT
optionC: MERGE
optionD: UPDATE
explanation:
DELETE is the command. On a Delta table it is a transactional operation that rewrites only the files containing rows that match the predicate, leaving every other file untouched — which is the selective behaviour the question describes.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (INSERT) — adds rows; it cannot remove any.
Option C (MERGE) — can delete as part of a conditional upsert against a source table, but it is far more machinery than a single predicate needs and there is no source relation here to merge from.
Option D (UPDATE) — modifies rows rather than removing them.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/delta-delete-from

question: A data engineer wants to schedule multiple tasks in a workflow where each task depends on the successful completion of previous tasks. The workflow should support retries and monitoring. Which Databricks feature should be used?
optionA: DBFS
optionB: Databricks Jobs
optionC: Delta Lake
optionD: Spark UI
explanation:
Databricks Jobs is the orchestrator. A job holds multiple tasks, each task can declare the tasks it depends on so ordering is explicit, and the platform supplies retry policies, notifications and per-run monitoring — every capability the question lists.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (DBFS) — a filesystem abstraction; it schedules nothing.
Option C (Delta Lake) — the storage format, not a scheduler.
Option D (Spark UI) — a diagnostic view of a single application's execution; it sequences no work.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/

question:
A data engineer needs to create a table in Databricks using data from their organization's existing SQLite database. They run the following command:
```sql
CREATE TABLE jdbc_customer360
USING _____
OPTIONS (
  url "jdbc:sqlite:/customers.db",
  dbtable "customer360"
)
```
Which of the following lines of code fills in the above blank to successfully complete the task?
optionA: org.apache.spark.sql.jdbc
optionB: sqlite
optionC: autoloader
optionD: org.apache.spark.sql.sqlite
optionE: DELTA
explanation:
org.apache.spark.sql.jdbc fills the blank. Reading an external relational database goes through Spark's JDBC data source, named that way in the USING clause; the connection details — the JDBC url, the driver class and the table to read — are then supplied through OPTIONS.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (sqlite) — no such data source; SQLite is reached through JDBC like any other relational database, with the database-specific part in the connection URL.
Option C (autoloader) — not a USING format; Auto Loader is a streaming source (cloudFiles) for files, not databases.
Option D (org.apache.spark.sql.sqlite) — does not exist.
Option E (DELTA) — would declare the table as Delta rather than reading from SQLite.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-create-table-using

question: A data engineer wants to create an external table in Databricks that references data stored in an Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) location. The goal is to enable Databricks to access and query this external data without moving it into the Databricks-managed storage. Which step should the data engineer take to successfully create the external table?
optionA: Use the CREATE MANAGED TABLE statement and specify the LOCATION clause with the path to the external data.
optionB: CREATE UNMANAGED TABLE statement without specifying a LOCATION clause.
optionC: Use the CREATE TABLE statement and specify the LOCATION clause with the path to the external data.
optionD: CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE statement without specifying a LOCATION clause.
explanation:
Using the CREATE TABLE statement with a LOCATION clause pointing at the ADLS path is how the external table is created. A LOCATION clause is what makes a table external (unmanaged): the catalog entry references the data where it already sits, nothing is copied into Databricks-managed storage, and dropping the table later leaves the files in place.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (CREATE MANAGED TABLE with LOCATION) — not valid syntax, and a managed table is by definition one whose storage Databricks controls.
Option B (CREATE UNMANAGED TABLE without LOCATION) — not valid syntax, and without a LOCATION there is nothing external to point at.
Option D (CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE without LOCATION) — the EXTERNAL keyword is accepted only as a synonym when LOCATION is present; without a path the table cannot reference the ADLS data.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/external

question: A data engineer notices that a Spark job performing a join between a large table and a small lookup table is slow. The lookup table is only a few megabytes. Which Spark optimization technique should be applied to improve the performance of the join operation?
optionA: Shuffle join
optionB: Broadcast join
optionC: Cartesian join
optionD: Sort merge join
explanation:
A broadcast join is the right optimisation when one side of a join is small. Spark sends a full copy of the small table to every executor so each one can join its partitions locally, which removes the shuffle of the large table entirely — and at a few megabytes this lookup table is comfortably within broadcast range. In practice adaptive query execution often selects a broadcast automatically once it sees the runtime size, but the join hint makes the intent explicit.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (shuffle join) — repartitions both sides across the network by join key, the expensive behaviour being avoided.
Option C (Cartesian join) — not an optimisation at all; it pairs every row with every other row.
Option D (sort merge join) — Spark's default for two large tables; it shuffles and sorts both sides, which the small lookup makes unnecessary.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-hints
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/optimizations/aqe

question: A data engineer wants to create a data entity from a couple of tables. The data entity must be used by other data engineers in other sessions. It also must be saved to a physical location. Which of the following data entities should the data engineer create?
optionA: Table
optionB: Database
optionC: View
optionD: Function
optionE: Temporary view
explanation:
A table is the only entity here that both persists to a physical location and is visible to other users in other sessions. It is registered in the metastore, so anyone with the right privileges can query it later, and its data is written to storage rather than recomputed.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Database) — a container for tables rather than a data entity built from them.
Option C (View) — shared across sessions, but a saved query that materialises nothing, so it stores no data of its own.
Option D (Function) — encapsulates logic, not data.
Option E (Temporary view) — fails both halves: no storage, and it disappears when the session ends.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/managed
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/views/

question: Which of the following describes the storage organization of a Delta table?
optionA: Delta tables are stored in a collection of files that contain data, history, metadata, and other attributes.
optionB: Delta tables store their data in a single file and all metadata in a collection of files in a separate location.
optionC: Delta tables are stored in a single file that contains data, history, metadata, and other attributes.
optionD: Delta tables are stored in a single file that contains only the data stored within the table.
optionE: Delta tables are stored in a collection of files that contain only the data stored within the table.
explanation:
Delta tables are stored in a collection of files that contain data, history, metadata and other attributes. A Delta table is a directory, not a file: the data lives in a collection of Parquet files, and beside them a _delta_log directory holds the transaction log — JSON commits plus periodic checkpoints — recording schema, metadata, statistics and the full version history. That structure is what makes time travel, ACID guarantees and data skipping work.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (single data file, metadata elsewhere) — the data is many Parquet files, and the log sits inside the table directory.
Option C (single file with everything) — nothing about Delta is a single file.
Option D (single file, data only) — wrong on both counts.
Option E (collection of files, data only) — leaves out the transaction log, without which there is no history, no metadata and no transactions.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/delta/

question: A data engineer needs to ingest streaming data from Kafka into a Delta Lake table using Databricks. The pipeline must guarantee exactly-once processing semantics and maintain checkpoint information to recover from failures. Which Spark Structured Streaming feature ensures reliable processing and fault tolerance?
optionA: Checkpointing
optionB: Watermarking
optionC: Caching
optionD: Partition pruning
explanation:
Checkpointing is what makes a streaming query recoverable. The checkpoint location stores the offsets processed in each batch along with the query's state, so after a failure the stream restarts from exactly where it stopped — and combined with a replayable source such as Kafka and an idempotent sink such as Delta, that is what delivers exactly-once semantics.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Watermarking) — bounds how late an event may arrive and lets state be discarded; it governs correctness over event time rather than recovery.
Option C (Caching) — keeps data in memory for reuse and does not survive a restart.
Option D (Partition pruning) — skips irrelevant files at read time; it tracks no progress.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/structured-streaming/checkpoints

question: A Databricks single-task workflow fails at the last task due to an error in a notebook. The data engineer fixes the mistake in the notebook. What should the data engineer do to rerun the workflow?
optionA: Repair the task
optionB: Rerun the pipeline
optionC: Restart the cluster
optionD: Switch the cluster
explanation:
Repairing the task is what reruns the workflow after the fix. When a job run fails partway through, Databricks lets you repair that run rather than start a fresh one: a repair re-executes only the failed and skipped tasks, reusing the successful output of everything upstream. In the Databricks UI the action is called Repair run and is initiated from the failed run; on a single-task workflow the distinction is cosmetic, since the one task is the whole run.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (rerun the pipeline) — would work but starts a fresh run rather than repairing the failed one.
Option C (restart the cluster) — the failure came from the notebook code, not the compute; new compute runs the same fixed code no faster.
Option D (switch the cluster) — the same, with a reconfiguration step added.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/repair-job-failures

question: A data engineer has written a function in a Databricks Notebook to calculate the population of bacteria in a given medium. Analysts use this function in the notebook and sometimes provide input arguments of the wrong data type, which can cause errors during execution. Which Databricks feature will help the data engineer quickly identify if an incorrect data type has been provided as input?
optionA: The Spark User interface has a debug tab that contains the variables that are used in this session.
optionB: The Databricks debugger enables breakpoints that will raise an error if the wrong data type is submitted.
optionC: The Databricks debugger enables the use of a variable explorer to see at a glance the value of the variables.
optionD: The Data Engineer should add print statements to find out what the variable is.
explanation:
