The Databricks debugger's variable explorer, which shows the value of variables at a glance, is the feature that catches a wrong-typed argument. Databricks notebooks include a built-in interactive debugger for Python, and the documentation describes what it provides: breakpoints, step-by-step execution and variable inspection. Variable values are shown in the variable explorer pane in the right sidebar, and local variables inside a function appear there marked [local] as you step through it. Seeing the value — and therefore the type — of an argument at a glance is exactly how you catch an analyst passing a string where a number was expected.
The old key claimed that breakpoints "will raise an error if the wrong data type is submitted". Breakpoints do no such thing: the documentation is explicit that when the code reaches a breakpoint it stops before the line is run, which is a pause, not a type check.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a Spark UI debug tab with session variables) — the Spark UI has no such tab; it shows jobs, stages and executors.
Option B (breakpoints raise an error on a wrong type) — a breakpoint pauses execution; nothing about it validates argument types.
Option D (add print statements) — the manual workaround the debugger exists to replace.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/notebooks/debugger

corrected.note: The debugger documentation lists variable inspection via the variable explorer pane, and states that a breakpoint stops execution before the line runs. The old key attributed type-checking behaviour to breakpoints, which they do not perform -- an invented mechanism rather than a documented one.

question: A data engineer wants to reduce costs and optimize cloud spending. The data engineer has decided to use Databricks Serverless for lowering cloud costs while maintaining existing SLAs. What is the first step in migrating to Databricks Serverless?
optionA: Legacy Ingestion pipelines that include ingestion from sources API's, files, JDBC/ODBC connections
optionB: A frequently running and efficient Python-based data transformation pipeline compatible with the latest Databricks runtime and Unity Catalog
optionC: A frequently running and efficient Scala-based data transformation pipeline compatible with the latest Databricks runtime and Unity Catalog
optionD: Low frequency BI Dashboarding and Adhoc SQL Analytics
explanation:
A frequently running, efficient Python-based transformation pipeline already compatible with the latest Databricks Runtime and Unity Catalog is the workload to migrate first. Those are the ones that move to serverless most safely — current runtime, Unity Catalog in place — and running often enough that removing cluster start-up time pays back immediately.
Python rather than Scala matters because serverless carries language-sensitive restrictions: user-defined code including UDFs, map and mapPartitions is capped at 1 GB of memory, Scala UDFs cannot be used inside higher-order functions, and CREATE FUNCTION (External) is unsupported.
Treat this item as weakly worded: it asks for a "first step" but every option names a workload rather than a step, and Databricks does not publish a prescribed migration order.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (legacy ingestion over APIs, files and JDBC/ODBC) — the most likely to run into serverless networking constraints, so the worst first candidate.
Option C (the same pipeline in Scala) — likelier to hit a serverless limitation during migration because of the Scala UDF restrictions above.
Option D (low-frequency BI and ad-hoc SQL) — gains little, since it spends most of its time idle.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/serverless/limitations
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/serverless/

corrected.note: Answer stands as the best-supported option. Grounded the Python-over-Scala preference in the documented serverless restrictions on user code, and flagged that the stem asks for a step while the options list workloads -- Databricks publishes no prescribed migration sequence.

question: In order for Structured Streaming to reliably track the exact progress of the processing so that it can handle any kind of failure by restarting and/or reprocessing, which of the following two approaches is used by Spark to record the offset range of the data being processed in each trigger?
optionA: Structured Streaming cannot record the offset range of the data being processed in each trigger.
optionB: Replayable Sources and Idempotent Sinks
optionC: Checkpointing and Write-ahead Logs
optionD: Write-ahead Logs and Idempotent Sinks
optionE: Checkpointing and Idempotent Sinks
explanation:
Checkpointing and write-ahead logs are the two approaches Spark uses to record the offset range of each trigger. The range being processed is written to the checkpoint's log ahead of the batch, so after any failure the engine can identify precisely which range was in flight and restart or reprocess it correctly.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (cannot record the offset range) — false; recording it is the whole purpose of the checkpoint log.
Option B (replayable sources and idempotent sinks) — the other half of end-to-end exactly-once delivery: properties of the source and sink that let a reprocessed batch land without duplicates, not the mechanism that records offsets.
Option D (write-ahead logs and idempotent sinks) — half right; the sink property is not how offsets are recorded.
Option E (checkpointing and idempotent sinks) — the same half-right pairing.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/structured-streaming/checkpoints

question: A data engineer is working on a personal laptop and needs to perform complex transformations on data stored in a Delta Lake on cloud storage. The engineer decides to use Databricks Connect to interact with Databricks clusters and work in their local IDE. How does Databricks Connect enable the engineer to develop, test, and debug code seamlessly on their local machine while interacting with Databricks clusters?
optionA: By providing a local environment that mimics the Databricks runtime, enabling the engineer to develop, test, and debug code using a specific IDE that is required by Databricks
optionB: By providing a local environment that mimics the Databricks runtime, enabling the engineer to develop, test, and debug code only through Databricks' own web interface
optionC: By allowing direct execution of Spark jobs from the local machine without needing a network connection
optionD: By providing a local environment that mimics the Databricks runtime, enabling the engineer to develop, test, and debug code using their preferred IDE
explanation:
Providing a local environment that mimics the Databricks runtime so the engineer can develop, test and debug in their preferred IDE is how Databricks Connect works. The client library runs in the local IDE — PyCharm, VS Code, IntelliJ, or any editor — and sends Spark work to a remote Databricks cluster or serverless compute for execution, so local tooling and remote scale coexist.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (a specific IDE required by Databricks) — no IDE is mandated; the point is to use whichever one the engineer prefers.
Option B (only through Databricks' own web interface) — the opposite of the feature's purpose, which is to leave the web notebook UI for a local editor.
Option C (execution without a network connection) — Databricks Connect executes on the remote cluster, so a connection to the workspace is required.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/databricks-connect/

question: A data engineer is working in a Python notebook on Databricks to process data, but notices that the output is not as expected. The data engineer wants to investigate the issue by stepping through the code and checking the values of certain variables during execution. Which tool should the data engineer use to inspect the code execution and variables in real-time?
optionA: Cluster Logs
optionB: Job Execution Dashboard
optionC: Python Notebook Interactive Debugger
optionD: SQL Analytics
explanation:
The Python Notebook Interactive Debugger is the tool. It lets the engineer set breakpoints, step through code execution and inspect variable values in real time, which is what diagnosing unexpected output inside a Databricks Python notebook requires.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Cluster Logs) — driver and executor logs record what ran; they cannot pause execution or show live variable values.
Option B (Job Execution Dashboard) — shows run status and timing for jobs, not the state of code inside a notebook cell.
Option D (SQL Analytics) — the SQL query and dashboard surface; it does not debug Python.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/notebooks/debugger

question: A data engineer is working on a Databricks project that utilizes cloud storage. The data engineer wants to load several JSON files from containers on a storage account as soon as the file arrives within the storage account. Which syntax should the data engineer follow to first load the files into a dataframe and check that it is working as expected using Python?
optionA:
```python
df = spark.read.json("input/path")
```
optionB:
```python
df = spark.readStream.format("cloud").option("json").load("/input/path")
```
optionC:
```python
df = spark.readStream.format("json".load("input/path")
```
optionD:
```python
df = spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles").option("cloudFiles.format", "json").load("/input/path")
```
explanation:
df = spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles").option("cloudFiles.format", "json").load("/input/path") is the syntax. That is Auto Loader: the cloudFiles source watches the storage path, picks up each new JSON file as it arrives, and returns a streaming DataFrame the engineer can display to confirm the load is working.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (spark.read.json) — a one-off batch read; it does not keep loading files as they arrive.
Option B (format("cloud").option("json")) — "cloud" is not a data source, and .option("json") supplies no key-value pair.
Option C (format("json".load(...))) — malformed: the closing parenthesis is missing, and a plain json stream is not Auto Loader.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ingestion/cloud-object-storage/auto-loader/

question: A data engineer wants to create a relational object by pulling data from two tables. The relational object does not need to be used by other data engineers in other sessions. In order to save on storage costs, the data engineer wants to avoid copying and storing physical data. Which of the following relational objects should the data engineer create?
optionA: Spark SQL Table
optionB: Delta Table
optionC: View
optionD: Database
optionE: Temporary view
explanation:
A temporary view fits both constraints exactly. It stores no data — it is a saved query evaluated when referenced, so there is no copy and no storage cost — and it is scoped to the session, which the question explicitly permits since nobody else needs it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Spark SQL Table) — materialises and stores the data, the cost the question is trying to avoid.
Option B (Delta Table) — the same; a table persists a physical copy.
Option C (View) — the closest distractor: it also avoids copying data, but it persists in the metastore for other sessions, which the requirement says is unnecessary.
Option D (Database) — a container, not a queryable object built from two tables.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/views/

question: A data engineer has inherited a Databricks pipeline from a previous team. The pipeline is missing SLAs and costs more than the allotted budget. On analysis, it is noted that the cluster is not being fully utilized, and the dataset is getting skewed. How should the data engineer resolve this issue?
optionA: Use coalesce() on the dataset to merge partitions and reduce skew.
optionB: Increase the number of executors for the job.
optionC: Repartition the dataset to have it be more optimally spread across all nodes.
optionD: Increase the executor memory for the job.
explanation:
Repartitioning the dataset so it is spread more evenly across all nodes is the fix. Repartition redistributes rows across partitions with a full shuffle, which directly addresses the two symptoms described: skew means a few partitions hold most of the data, which is also why the cluster looks underused — most executors finish early and idle while a handful of stragglers run on.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (coalesce() to merge partitions) — the trap: it reduces the partition count without a full shuffle, which makes uneven distribution worse rather than better.
Option B (more executors) — scales the cluster up without fixing the imbalance; the stragglers stay stragglers and the bill grows.
Option D (more executor memory) — the same; memory does not redistribute skewed data.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/optimizations/

question: A data engineer is configuring a cluster in Databricks and wants to ensure that multiple Spark executors can run tasks concurrently across worker nodes. Which cluster component is responsible for executing tasks?
optionA: Driver
optionB: Notebook
optionC: Executor
optionD: Job scheduler
explanation:
Executors are the processes that run tasks. Each worker node hosts one or more executors, each executor has a number of cores, and Spark schedules one task per core — so concurrency across the cluster comes from the executors, and adding workers or cores is what raises it.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Driver) — the coordinator: it builds the execution plan, splits stages into tasks and hands them out, but does not run them (a single-node cluster is the exception, where the driver also acts as the worker).
Option B (Notebook) — an authoring surface, not a runtime component.
Option D (Job scheduler) — decides when work runs rather than executing it.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/spark/

question: A data engineer needs to optimize the data layout and query performance for an e-commerce transactions Delta table. The table is partitioned by "purchase_date" a date column which helps with time-based queries but does not optimize searches on user statistics "customer_id", a high- cardinality column. The table is usually queried with filters on "customer_id" within specific date ranges, but since this data is spread across multiple files in each partition, it results in full partition scans and increased runtime and costs. How should the data engineer optimize the Data Layout for efficient reads?
optionA: Alter table implementing liquid clustering on "customer_id" while keeping the existing partitioning.
optionB: Alter the table implementing liquid clustering by "customer_id" and "purchase_date".
optionC: Alter the table to partition by "customer_id".
optionD: Enable delta caching on the cluster so that frequent reads are cached for performance.
explanation:
Altering the table to use liquid clustering by customer_id and purchase_date is the optimisation. Queries filter on customer_id within purchase_date ranges, so clustering on both keys lets Delta lay out and skip files along both dimensions; liquid clustering handles a high-cardinality key like customer_id without the small-file explosion that static partitioning on it would cause, and it can be applied to the existing table with ALTER TABLE ... CLUSTER BY.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (liquid clustering on customer_id while keeping the partitioning) — liquid clustering is not compatible with partitioning; a table uses one or the other, and dropping purchase_date from the clustering key loses the time-range skipping.
Option C (partition by customer_id) — a high-cardinality partition key produces a huge number of tiny partitions and files, which Databricks explicitly advises against.
Option D (enable Delta caching) — speeds repeat reads of the same files on the same cluster; it does nothing about the layout that forces full partition scans in the first place.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/clustering

question: A data engineer needs to provide access to a group named manufacturing-team. The team needs privileges to create tables in the quality schema. Which set of SQL commands will grant a group named manufacturing-team to create tables in a schema named production with the parent catalog named manufacturing with the least privileges?
explanation:
GRANT CREATE TABLE ON SCHEMA manufacturing.quality, GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA manufacturing.quality and GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG manufacturing is the least-privilege set. Creating a table needs CREATE TABLE on the schema, plus the traversal privileges USE SCHEMA on the schema and USE CATALOG on its parent; nothing else is required. (The stem names both "quality" and "production" as the schema; the options all use manufacturing.quality, so read it that way.)
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (USE TABLE instead of CREATE TABLE) — USE TABLE is not a privilege, and nothing in the set allows creating anything.
Option C (CREATE TABLE, CREATE SCHEMA, CREATE CATALOG) — grants the ability to create schemas and catalogs, well beyond what the team needs, and omits the USE privileges that let them reach the schema at all.
Option D (CREATE TABLE, CREATE SCHEMA, USE CATALOG) — CREATE SCHEMA on a schema is meaningless (it is a catalog-level privilege) and USE SCHEMA is missing.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/access-control/privileges-reference

question: A data engineer is implementing a data pipeline using Databricks notebooks. The engineer wants to share parameters such as file paths and processing dates across multiple tasks within a job. Which Databricks utility enables parameter passing?
optionA: display
optionB: dbutils.widgets
optionC: spark.conf
optionD: dbutils.fs
explanation:
dbutils.widgets is the parameter mechanism. Widgets declare named inputs on a notebook, a job task supplies values for them at run time, and the notebook reads them with dbutils.widgets.get — so the same notebook can be reused across tasks and runs with different file paths and processing dates.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (display) — renders output; it passes nothing in.
Option C (spark.conf) — the closest distractor: it holds key-value settings, but it configures a Spark session rather than parameterising a task, and job task parameters are not passed through it.
Option D (dbutils.fs) — works with files, not parameters.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/notebooks/widgets

question: A new data engineering team team. has been assigned to an ELT project. The new data engineering team will need full privileges on the database customers to fully manage the project. Which of the following commands can be used to grant full permissions on the database to the new data engineering team?
explanation:
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE customers TO team; grants the full set of privileges on the database in one statement, which is what "full permissions" asks for.
One currency note: DATABASE is legacy Hive metastore vocabulary. Under Unity Catalog the equivalent object is a schema, and the same grant reads GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON SCHEMA <catalog>.<schema> TO <principal>.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (ON DATABASE team TO customers) — inverts the principal and the securable; the object comes after ON, the principal after TO.
Option C (SELECT CREATE MODIFY USAGE PRIVILEGES) — strings privileges together without commas and misuses the PRIVILEGES keyword; it does not parse.
Option D (SELECT PRIVILEGES ... TO teams) — read access only, with the same keyword misuse, and a principal that does not match the group.
Option E (USAGE only) — the traversal privilege alone; the team could see the database but not manage anything in it.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/access-control/privileges-reference

question: A data engineer is migrating pipeline tasks to reduce operational toil. The workspace used Unity Catalog and is in a region that supports serverless. The engineer wants Databricks to auto-select instance types, manage scaling, apply Photon, and handle runtime upgrades automatically for job runs. How should the data engineer meet this requirement while adhering to Databricks constraints?
optionA: Run the job on a serverless compute for workflows configuration, ensuring Unity Catalog is enabled and regional support is available.
optionB: Use a Pro SQL warehouse and schedule Python notebook tasks to execute as pipeline steps.
optionC: Create a job with a single-task job cluster and manually set instance families and min/max workers.
optionD: Use an all-purpose cluster with cluster policies to enforce standard sizes and enable autoscaling.
explanation:
Running the job on serverless compute for workflows, with Unity Catalog enabled and regional support confirmed, is how Databricks takes over instance selection, scaling, Photon and runtime upgrades. Serverless job compute is fully managed: there is no instance type or worker count to choose, Photon is on, and the runtime is upgraded by Databricks — and the two constraints named in the option are the documented prerequisites.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Pro SQL warehouse running Python notebook tasks) — a SQL warehouse runs SQL, not notebook tasks, and Pro is classic compute the customer still sizes.
Option C (single-task job cluster with manual instance families and min/max workers) — the engineer picks every setting by hand, the toil the migration is meant to remove.
Option D (all-purpose cluster with policies and autoscaling) — policies standardise sizes but do not auto-select them, all-purpose compute is the expensive choice for jobs, and runtime upgrades stay manual.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/serverless/

question: A data engineer only wants to execute the final block of a Python program if the Python variable day_of_week is equal to 1 and the Python variable review_period is True. Which of the following control flow statements should the data engineer use to begin this conditionally executed code block?
optionA: if day_of_week = 1 & review_period: = "True":
optionB: if day_of_week == 1 and review_period == "True":
optionC: if day_of_week = 1 and review_period:
optionD: if day_of_week == 1 and review_period:
optionE: if day_of_week = 1 and review_period = "True":
explanation:
if day_of_week == 1 and review_period: is the line. Python needs == for comparison and the keyword and for the boolean operator, and because review_period is already a boolean, testing it directly is the idiomatic form — no comparison is needed.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (= 1 & review_period: = "True") — single = is assignment, & is the bitwise operator, and the stray : = is not Python.
Option B (== 1 and review_period == "True") — syntactically valid and still wrong: it compares the boolean against the string "True", which is False even when the variable is True, since True and "True" are different types.
Option C (= 1 and review_period) — single = is assignment, a syntax error inside an if.
Option E (= 1 and review_period = "True") — two assignments where comparisons are needed.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/pyspark/

question: A data engineering team wants to validate a new ingestion pipeline locally while ensuring large aggregations run in serverless compute in their Databricks workspace. They plan to use Databricks Connect and have the option to attach to either a shared cluster or serverless. Which workspace requirement should be confirmed first to avoid connection failures?
optionA: Verify that the workspace has Unity Catalog disabled and the Databricks Connect version is less than the serverless Runtime version.
optionB: Verify that the workspace has Unity Catalog enabled and that the Databricks Connect version supports serverless for the target Runtime release.
optionC: Verify that only assigned access mode clusters are used because serverless is not supported by Databricks Connect.
optionD: Verify that the local Spark version equals the serverless Spark version to satisfy Spark Connect parity.
explanation:
Verifying that the workspace has Unity Catalog enabled and that the Databricks Connect version supports serverless for the target Runtime release is the requirement to confirm first. Databricks Connect requires Unity Catalog to connect to serverless compute, and serverless support arrived in specific Databricks Connect versions, so a client too old for the target release fails to connect.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Unity Catalog disabled, client version lower than the runtime) — backwards on both counts: Unity Catalog is required, and the client must be new enough, not older.
Option C (only assigned-mode clusters, serverless unsupported) — false; Databricks Connect supports serverless compute.
Option D (local Spark version equal to the serverless Spark version) — Databricks Connect uses Spark Connect precisely so the local machine needs no matching Spark installation.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/databricks-connect/

question: A data analyst has a series of queries in a SQL program. The data analyst wants this program to run every day. They only want the final query in the program to run on Sundays. They ask for help from the data engineering team to complete this task. Which of the following approaches could be used by the data engineering team to complete this task?
optionA: They could submit a feature request with Databricks to add this functionality.
optionB: They could automatically restrict access to the source table in the final query so that it is only accessible on Sundays.
optionC: They could redesign the data model to separate the data used in the final query into a new table.
optionD: They could only run the entire program on Sundays.
optionE: They could wrap the queries using PySpark and use Python's control flow system to determine when to run the final query.
explanation:
Wrapping the queries in PySpark and using Python's control flow to decide when the final query runs is the approach. SQL alone has no conditional execution across statements, so driving the queries from Python — each through spark.sql() — lets ordinary control flow check the weekday and execute the last query only on Sundays.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (submit a feature request) — concedes the task is impossible when it is not.
Option B (restrict access to the source table except on Sundays) — enforces timing through permissions, which makes the query fail rather than be skipped, and is a fragile way to express a schedule.
Option C (redesign the data model) — does not address when a query runs.
Option D (run the entire program only on Sundays) — loses the daily cadence the analyst needs.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/pyspark/

question: A data engineer is configuring Unity Catalog in Databricks and needs to assign a role to a user who should have the ability to grant and revoke privileges on various data objects within a specific schema, but should not have read/write access over the schema or its objects. Which role should the data engineer assign to this user?
optionA: Table Owner
optionB: Catalog Owner
optionC: Schema Owner
optionD: USE catalog/schema privilege on the schema
explanation:
Schema Owner is the role to assign. In Unity Catalog the owner of an object can grant and revoke privileges on it and on the objects beneath it, so making the user the owner of the schema gives them grant and revoke authority scoped to that schema alone. This is the exam's framing; note that Databricks documents owners as holding all privileges on what they own, so treat "no read/write access" as a statement about the intent of the role rather than a hard technical guarantee.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Table Owner) — scoped to one table; cannot manage privileges on the other objects in the schema.
Option B (Catalog Owner) — too broad: authority over every schema in the catalog, not the one specified.
Option D (USE CATALOG / USE SCHEMA) — traversal privileges only; they let a user reach the schema but confer no ability to grant or revoke anything.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/manage-privileges

question: A data engineer needs to append new records to an existing Delta table while preserving existing data. The ingestion pipeline runs every hour and adds incremental data without replacing previous records. Which write mode should be used?
optionA: append
optionB: errorIfExists
optionC: overwrite
optionD: ignore
explanation:
append is the write mode: it adds the new rows and leaves existing data in place, which is what an hourly incremental load needs.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (errorIfExists) — the default for a DataFrame write; it fails outright once the table exists, so the second hourly run would break.
Option C (overwrite) — replaces the table's contents, discarding every previously loaded record.
Option D (ignore) — silently does nothing when the table exists, so the pipeline would appear to succeed while loading no data — the most dangerous of the three, because nothing signals the failure.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-dml-insert-into

question: What is the functionality of AutoLoader in Databricks?
optionA: Auto Loader automatically ingests and processes new files from cloud storage, handling both batch and streaming data with support for schema evolution.
optionB: Auto Loader automatically ingests and processes new files from cloud storage, handling batch and streaming data with no support for schema evolution.
optionC: Auto Loader automatically ingests and processes new files from cloud storage, handling only streaming data with no support for schema evolution.
optionD: Auto Loader automatically ingests and processes new files from cloud storage, handling batch data with support for schema evolution.
explanation:
Auto Loader automatically ingests and processes new files from cloud storage, handling both batch and streaming data with support for schema evolution — both halves matter, and only one option states both.
On batch versus streaming: Auto Loader is built on Structured Streaming and provides the cloudFiles source, but a query using it can be triggered to run periodically rather than continuously. Trigger.AvailableNow processes whatever files have accumulated and then stops, which is how Auto Loader serves scheduled batch ingestion without ceasing to be a streaming source. On schema evolution: the behaviour is controlled by cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode, whose default adds newly discovered columns to the schema, with modes available to rescue unexpected columns, fail on them, or ignore them.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (batch and streaming, no schema evolution) — schema evolution is a documented, default-on feature.
Option C (only streaming, no schema evolution) — wrong on both counts; AvailableNow gives batch-style runs, and evolution is supported.
Option D (batch only, with schema evolution) — Auto Loader is a streaming source first; the batch usage is a triggering choice on top of it.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ingestion/cloud-object-storage/auto-loader/
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ingestion/cloud-object-storage/auto-loader/schema

question: A data engineer needs to conduct Exploratory Analysis on data residing in a database that is within the company's custom-defined network in the cloud. The data engineer is using SQL for this task. Which type of SQL Warehouse will enable the data engineer to process large numbers of queries quickly and cost-effectively?
optionA: Serverless compute for notebooks
optionB: Pro SQL Warehouse
optionC: Classic SQL Warehouse
optionD: Serverless SQL Warehouse
explanation:
A Serverless SQL Warehouse is the type that processes large numbers of queries quickly and cost-effectively — that phrase is lifted from the Databricks warehouse-types documentation. Intelligent Workload Management is described there as a set of features that enhances Databricks SQL Serverless's ability to process large numbers of queries quickly and cost-effectively, using AI-powered prediction and dynamic management rather than static thresholds, and the feature table lists IWM against Serverless only. Serverless also starts in roughly two to six seconds and upscales rapidly, so it absorbs a burst of exploratory queries without paying for idle capacity.
A note on the stem: the reference to a custom-defined network reads as though it should favour a warehouse running inside the customer VPC, but the question asks specifically about processing many queries quickly and cost-effectively, which is the documented IWM wording and therefore Serverless.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (serverless compute for notebooks) — compute for notebook workloads, not a SQL warehouse type at all.
Option B (Pro SQL Warehouse) — runs in the classic compute plane, gets Photon and Predictive IO but not IWM, and must spin up before answering.
Option C (Classic SQL Warehouse) — the same, with Photon alone.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/sql-warehouse/warehouse-types

corrected.note: The documentation attributes Intelligent Workload Management -- worded almost exactly as the question is -- to Serverless SQL warehouses only. A near-duplicate of this item elsewhere in the deck already keys Serverless, so the two now agree.

question: A data engineer needs to use a Delta table as part of a data pipeline, but they do not know if they have the appropriate permissions. In which of the following locations can the data engineer review their permissions on the table?
optionA: Jobs
optionB: Dashboards
optionC: Databricks Filesystem
optionD: Repos
optionE: Data Explorer
explanation:
Data Explorer is where the engineer reviews their permissions on the table. Opening the table there shows its owner and its granted privileges, which is how an engineer checks whether they already hold the access they need.
One naming note: Databricks has renamed Data Explorer to Catalog Explorer, so on a current workspace this is the Catalog Explorer entry in the sidebar. The answer is unchanged; only the label has moved. A near-duplicate of this question elsewhere in the deck uses the newer name.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Jobs) — lists and configures workflows; it shows no table privileges.
Option B (Dashboards) — a visualisation surface.
Option C (Databricks Filesystem) — a file view; Unity Catalog privileges are on the table object, not the files.
Option D (Repos) — Git-backed code folders.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/discover/database-objects

corrected.note: Answer stands. Recorded that Data Explorer is now called Catalog Explorer, since a learner following the old label will not find it in a current workspace.

question: What can be used to simplify and unify siloed data architectures that are specialized for specific use cases?
optionA: Delta Lake
optionB: Data lake
optionC: Data warehouse
optionD: Data lakehouse
explanation:
A data lakehouse is what simplifies and unifies siloed, use-case-specific architectures. It combines the best of data lakes and data warehouses so structured and unstructured data coexist in one governed system, serving analytics, machine learning and business intelligence from the same copy rather than from separate specialised stacks.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Delta Lake) — the storage layer that brings reliability to a data lake; a lakehouse is the broader architecture built on it.
Option B (Data lake) — stores large volumes of raw data but lacks the structure and performance for high-performance analytics, so it is one of the silos rather than the unifier.
Option C (Data warehouse) — designed for structured data and BI, not for large volumes of unstructured or semi-structured data; the other silo.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/

question: A data engineer is standardizing repository layouts for multiple teams adopting Databricks Asset Bundles. The engineer wants to ensure every project has a single authoritative configuration file at the repository root that defines the bundle name, targets, workspace settings, permissions, and resource mappings (for jobs and pipelines). What strategy should the data engineer use to meet the goal?
optionA: Place multiple databricks.ymlfiles under each subfolder (for example, jobs/pipelines/, workspace/) and merge them at deploy time using the include mapping.
optionB: Place exactly one databricks.yml at the repository root; it is the main configuration file and may reference additional configuration files via the include mapping.
optionC: Place a databricks.ymlin a databricks/hidden folder at the repository root; only hidden locations are valid for bundle configs.
optionD: Place a databricks.yaml at the repository root and optional databricks.yml in subfolders; the CLI prefers .yamlover .ymlwhen both exist.
explanation:
Placing exactly one databricks.yml at the repository root, as the main configuration file that may reference additional configuration files via the include mapping, is the strategy. Bundles require a single databricks.yml at the root that defines the bundle name, targets, workspace settings, permissions and resources; modularisation is done by listing further YAML files under include, which the root file pulls in.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (multiple databricks.yml files under subfolders merged by include) — there is one root databricks.yml; included files are additional configuration, not additional databricks.yml files.
Option C (a databricks.yml in a hidden folder) — the file must be at the bundle root; hidden folders are not a requirement or a valid location.
Option D (databricks.yaml at root, CLI prefers .yaml) — the documented filename is databricks.yml, and there is no preference rule between extensions.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/bundles/

question: Which of the following statements regarding the relationship between Silver tables and Bronze tables is always true?
optionA: Silver tables contain more data than Bronze tables.
optionB: Silver tables contain a more refined and cleaner view of data than Bronze tables.
optionC: Silver tables contain less data than Bronze tables.
optionD: Silver tables contain a less refined, less clean view of data than Bronze data.
optionE: Silver tables contain aggregates while Bronze data is unaggregated.
explanation:
Silver tables contain a more refined and cleaner view of data than Bronze tables — the only claim that always holds. That is the definition of the layers: Bronze keeps source data as it arrived, Silver applies cleaning, conforming and deduplication.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Silver contains more data) — not guaranteed; deduplication and filtering often make Silver smaller.
Option C (Silver contains less data) — not guaranteed either; joins and enrichment can add columns, and a Silver table built from several Bronze sources may be larger outright.
Option D (Silver is less refined) — inverts the architecture.
Option E (Silver holds aggregates) — aggregation is characteristic of Gold, not Silver.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

question: A data engineering project involves processing large batches of data on a daily schedule using ETL. The jobs are resource-intensive and vary in size, requiring a scalable, cost-efficient compute solution that can automatically scale based on the workload. Which compute approach will satisfy the needs described?
optionA: Job Cluster
optionB: Dedicated Cluster
optionC: All-Purpose Cluster
optionD: Databricks SQL Serverless
explanation:
A Job Cluster is the compute approach. Job clusters are ephemeral: created for the scheduled run, sized by the job's configuration with autoscaling to match the workload, and terminated when the run completes, so nothing is paid for between daily batches — the fit for resource-intensive ETL that varies in size.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (Dedicated Cluster) — not a Databricks compute type as such; a dedicated (single-user) access mode is a setting, and a permanently dedicated cluster would sit idle between runs.
Option C (All-Purpose Cluster) — built for interactive work, stays up between uses and is billed at a higher rate; the expensive choice for scheduled ETL.
Option D (Databricks SQL Serverless) — runs SQL queries; it is not the compute for a general ETL job.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/compute

question: A data organization leader is upset about the data analysis team's reports being different from the data engineering team's reports. The leader believes the siloed nature of their organization's data engineering and data analysis architectures is to blame. Which of the following describes how a data lakehouse could alleviate this issue?
optionA: Both teams would be able to collaborate on projects in real-time
optionB: Both teams would reorganize to report to the same department
optionC: Both teams would use the same source of truth for their work
optionD: Both teams would autoscale their work as data size evolves
optionE: Both teams would respond more quickly to ad-hoc requests
explanation:
Both teams would use the same source of truth for their work, and that is what removes the disagreement. The reports differed because each team was working from its own extract in its own system; when the engineering pipeline and the analysts' queries read the same governed tables, the numbers reconcile by construction.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (collaborate in real time) — a genuine benefit that does not explain why two reports disagree.
Option B (reorganise to the same department) — an org change, not anything a lakehouse does.
Option D (autoscale as data grows) — real, but about capacity, not consistency.
Option E (respond faster to ad-hoc requests) — real, but faster answers from two sources would still be two different answers.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/

question: A data engineer wants to read only a subset of columns from a Delta table to reduce memory usage and improve performance. Which Spark DataFrame operation should be used?
optionA: filter
optionB: select
optionC: orderBy
optionD: groupBy
explanation:
select is the operation that reads only a subset of columns. It projects the named columns, and because Delta stores data in Parquet — a columnar format — Spark reads only the column chunks it actually needs. That column pruning is what reduces I/O and memory for a wide table.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (filter) — the close distractor: it prunes in the other dimension, removing rows rather than columns, so it does not reduce the number of columns read.
Option C (orderBy) — sorts and forces a shuffle, adding work rather than reducing what is read.
Option D (groupBy) — aggregates; it changes the shape of the result, not the columns scanned.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/pyspark/

question: A data engineer wants to store intermediate data in a temporary view for use within the same Spark session. The data should not persist after the session ends. Which Spark SQL command should be used?
optionA: CREATE TABLE
optionB: CREATE TEMP VIEW
optionC: CREATE VIEW
optionD: CREATE DATABASE
explanation:
CREATE TEMP VIEW registers a view scoped to the current Spark session. It stores no data, it is not written to the metastore, and it disappears when the session ends — exactly the lifetime the question describes for intermediate results.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (CREATE TABLE) — materialises and stores the data, which is more than intermediate results need, and persists after the session.
Option C (CREATE VIEW) — persists in the metastore and outlives the session, which the question rules out.
Option D (CREATE DATABASE) — makes a container, not a queryable object.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-create-view

question: A Python file is ready for production and the client wants to use the most efficient yet cost- effective type of cluster possible. The workload is quite small, only processing 10GBs of data with only simple joins and no complex aggregations or wide transformations. Which cluster meets the requirement?
optionA: Job cluster with spot instances enabled
optionB: Job cluster with Photon enabled
optionC: Job cluster with spot instances disabled
optionD: Interactive cluster
explanation:
A job cluster with spot instances enabled is the most cost-effective fit. A job cluster exists only for the duration of the run and is terminated afterwards, and spot instances cut the compute price further; for a small 10 GB workload with simple joins and no wide transformations, an occasional spot reclamation costs a cheap retry rather than a long rerun, and no performance add-on is needed.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (job cluster with Photon) — Photon accelerates heavy SQL and DataFrame work at a higher DBU rate; a small, simple workload does not earn it back.
Option C (job cluster with spot disabled) — on-demand only; pays more for a workload that tolerates spot interruption easily.
Option D (interactive cluster) — an all-purpose cluster stays up between runs and is billed at a higher rate, the wrong choice for a production file.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/compute

question: A data engineer is configuring a batch processing job in Databricks to read large Parquet datasets from cloud storage. The engineer wants Spark to automatically distribute computation across multiple worker nodes without manually assigning tasks. Which Spark abstraction enables automatic parallel processing?
optionA: Executor
optionB: Cluster
optionC: DataFrame
optionD: Driver
explanation:
The DataFrame is the abstraction that makes parallelism automatic. It represents a distributed collection partitioned across the cluster, and Spark's engine plans the work over those partitions and schedules tasks itself — so nobody assigns work to nodes by hand.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Executor) — the process that runs the resulting tasks; part of the machinery, not the abstraction that expresses the computation.
Option B (Cluster) — the pool of compute the tasks occupy.
Option D (Driver) — plans and coordinates the tasks; it is what schedules them, not what the engineer programs against.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/pyspark/

question: An organization needs to share a dataset stored in its Databricks Unity Catalog with an external partner who uses a different data platform that is not Databricks. The goal is to maintain data security and ensure the partner can access the data efficiently. Which method should the data engineer use to securely share the dataset with the external partner?
optionA: Using Delta Sharing with the open sharing protocol
optionB: Exporting data as CSV files and emailing them
optionC: Using a third-party API to access the Delta table
optionD: Databricks-to-Databricks Sharing
explanation:
Delta Sharing with the open sharing protocol is the method for a partner who is not on Databricks. The open protocol lets any client that implements it — pandas, Spark, Power BI, and others — read shared tables directly from the provider's cloud storage through short-lived credentials, while the share, its recipients and its audit trail stay governed in Unity Catalog.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (export CSV and email) — copies the data out of governance entirely, with no access control, no audit and no refresh.
Option C (a third-party API against the Delta table) — hands out direct access to the underlying storage or a bespoke integration, bypassing the share and its governance.
Option D (Databricks-to-Databricks sharing) — requires the recipient to have a Unity Catalog-enabled Databricks workspace, which this partner does not.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/opensharing/share-data-open

question: A data engineer notices that a Spark job repeatedly scans a large Delta table even though the dataset does not change during the session. Which technique can store the dataset in memory to speed up repeated queries?
optionA: VACUUM
optionB: MERGE
optionC: OPTIMIZE
optionD: CACHE TABLE
explanation:
CACHE TABLE materialises the table into cluster memory, so repeated queries in the same session read from memory instead of rescanning the files. That is the right tool when the data does not change during the session, which the question specifies.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (VACUUM) — deletes unreferenced old files and reclaims storage; nothing goes into memory.
Option B (MERGE) — performs conditional upserts.
Option C (OPTIMIZE) — the tempting distractor: it improves read performance by compacting small files on disk, rewriting the table rather than caching it.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-aux-cache-cache-table

question: A data engineer is working with a very large dataset and wants to improve query performance by colocating related data in the same files. The engineer decides to apply Z-ordering on frequently filtered columns. Which Delta Lake command is used?
optionA: ANALYZE TABLE
optionB: CACHE TABLE
optionC: OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY
optionD: VACUUM ZORDER
explanation:
OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (columns) is the command. OPTIMIZE rewrites the table's files, and the ZORDER BY clause decides how rows are colocated within them, so values that are queried together end up in the same files. That improves data skipping, because the per-file statistics in the transaction log then let Spark eliminate far more files for a filtered query.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (ANALYZE TABLE) — collects statistics without moving any data.
Option B (CACHE TABLE) — holds data in memory without changing its layout on disk.
Option D (VACUUM ZORDER) — not a command; Z-ordering is a clause of OPTIMIZE, and VACUUM only deletes unreferenced files.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/data-skipping

question: A data engineer is developing an ETL process based on Spark SQL. The execution fails. The data engineer checks the Spark UI and can see the ERRORS as follows: "java.lang.OutofMemoryError: Java heap space" Which two corrective actions should the data engineer perform to resolve this issue? (Choose two.)
optionA: Narrow the filters in order to collect less data in the query
optionB: Upsize the worker nodes and activate autoshuffle partitions
optionC: Upsize the driver node and deactivate autoshuffle partitions
optionD: Cache the dataset in order to boost the query performance
optionE: Fix the shuffle partitions to 50 to ensure the allocation
explanation:
Narrowing the filters to collect less data, and upsizing the worker nodes while activating auto shuffle partitions, are the two corrective actions. A Java heap OutOfMemoryError in a Spark SQL job means an executor (or the driver, on a collect) ran out of memory: reading less input lowers the pressure directly, and larger workers plus adaptive shuffle partitioning give each task more memory and right-sized partitions so no single task has to hold an oversized chunk.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option C (upsize the driver, deactivate auto shuffle partitions) — the heap that overflowed during a distributed query is on the executors, and turning adaptive partitioning off removes the mechanism that splits oversized partitions.
Option D (cache the dataset) — caching pins more data in memory, which makes an out-of-memory condition worse, not better.
Option E (fix shuffle partitions to 50) — a hard-coded low count means fewer, larger partitions per task, exactly the shape that overflows a heap.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/optimizations/

question: A data engineer is designing an ETL pipeline to process both streaming and batch data from multiple sources. The pipeline must ensure data quality, handle schema evolution, and provide easy maintenance. The team is considering using Delta Live Tables (DLT) in Databricks to achieve these goals. They want to understand the key features and benefits of DLT that make it suitable for this use case. Why is Delta Live Tables (DLT) an appropriate choice?
optionA: Automatic data quality checks, built-in support for schema evolution, and declarative pipeline development
optionB: Manual schema enforcement, high operational overhead, and limited scalability
optionC: Requires custom code for data quality checks, no support for streaming data, and complex pipeline maintenance
optionD: Supports only batch processing, no data versioning, and high infrastructure costs
explanation:
Automatic data quality checks, built-in support for schema evolution and declarative pipeline development are why Delta Live Tables fits. Expectations give the quality checks, the framework handles schema changes on streaming tables, and datasets are declared rather than orchestrated by hand — so the same pipeline serves both streaming and batch sources with less to maintain.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (manual schema enforcement, high overhead, limited scalability) — the opposite of DLT on every count.
Option C (custom code for quality, no streaming support, complex maintenance) — DLT is built on Structured Streaming and its expectations are declarative; none of this is true.
Option D (batch only, no versioning, high infrastructure cost) — DLT is streaming-first, writes Delta tables with full version history, and manages its own compute.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectations

question: A data engineer is reading a very large dataset that contains skewed key values. Some partitions contain significantly more records than others, causing uneven workload distribution across executors. Which Spark issue does this scenario describe?
optionA: Schema evolution
optionB: Data skew
optionC: Lazy evaluation
optionD: Broadcast failure
explanation:
Data skew is the issue described: the join or grouping key is distributed unevenly, so a few partitions hold far more records than the rest. The visible symptom is exactly what the question says — most executors finish quickly and idle while a handful of stragglers carry the bulk of the work, so the stage takes as long as its slowest partition.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (schema evolution) — about a changing schema, not data distribution.
Option C (lazy evaluation) — Spark's deferral of computation until an action is called; unrelated to partition sizes.
Option D (broadcast failure) — would concern a table too large to broadcast, not uneven partitioning.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/optimizations/

question: A data engineer needs to use a Delta table as part of a data pipeline, but they do not know if they have the appropriate permissions. In which location can the data engineer review their permissions on the table?
optionA: Jobs
optionB: Dashboards
optionC: Catalog Explorer
optionD: Repos
explanation:
Catalog Explorer is where a table's permissions are reviewed. Selecting the table shows its owner and the privileges granted on it, which answers whether the engineer already has the access their pipeline needs. Catalog Explorer is the current name for what earlier documentation called Data Explorer; a near-duplicate of this question elsewhere in the deck still uses the older label.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Jobs) — lists and configures workflows; no table-level privilege information.
Option B (Dashboards) — a visualisation surface.
Option D (Repos) — Git-backed code folders.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/discover/database-objects

question: A data engineer needs to access the view created by the sales team, using a shared cluster. The data engineer has been provided usage permissions on the catalog and schema. In order to access the view created by sales team. What are the minimum permissions the data engineer would require in addition?
optionA: Needs SELECT permission only on the VIEW
optionB: Needs SELECT permission on the VIEW and the underlying TABLE.
optionC: Needs ALL PRIVILEGES on the VIEW
optionD: Needs ALL PRIVILEGES at the SCHEMA level
explanation:
SELECT permission on the view only is the minimum. Unity Catalog resolves a view's underlying tables using the view owner's privileges, so a reader never needs access to the tables the view reads from — provided they can already traverse the catalog and schema, which the question grants. That indirection is what makes views useful for exposing a filtered or masked slice of data without exposing the source.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (SELECT on the view and the underlying table) — the natural but incorrect assumption; requiring table access would defeat the point of the view.
Option C (ALL PRIVILEGES on the view) — would work but grants far more than reading requires, which the question rules out by asking for the minimum.
Option D (ALL PRIVILEGES at the schema level) — the same, one level broader still.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/access-control/privileges-reference

question: A data engineer has a Job that has a complex run schedule, and they want to transfer that schedule to other Jobs. Rather than manually selecting each value in the scheduling form in Databricks, which of the following tools can the data engineer use to represent and submit the schedule programmatically?
optionA: There is no way to represent and submit this information programmatically
optionB: datetime
optionC: pyspark.sql.types.TimestampType
optionD: pyspark.sql.types.DateType
optionE: Cron syntax
explanation:
Cron syntax is how a job schedule is represented and submitted programmatically. A quartz cron string encodes the minute, hour, day and day-of-week pattern in a single line, and because it is just a string it can be copied between jobs, stored in a bundle's YAML, or submitted through the Jobs API — exactly the transferable representation the question asks for.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (no programmatic representation exists) — contradicted by the Jobs API, the CLI and bundles, all of which take the cron string.
Option B (datetime) — represents a single point in time, not a recurring pattern.
Option C (pyspark.sql.types.TimestampType) — a column data type; it cannot express "every weekday at 06:00".
Option D (pyspark.sql.types.DateType) — the same, for dates.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/triggers

question: A data engineer is onboarding a new bronze ingestion pipeline in Databricks with Unity Catalog. The team wants Databricks to handle storage layout, apply platform optimizations over time, and simplify lifecycle management so that when a table is dropped, its underlying data is also cleaned up according to Databricks-managed retention policies. Which table type should the data engineer create for these ingestion tables?
optionA: Managed tables so that Unity Catalog manages both metadata and underlying data lifecycle.
optionB: External tables with a LOCATION pointing to an external volume for full control of file layout.
optionC: Foreign tables federated from an external catalog to delegate optimization to the source system.
optionD: Temporary views over files to avoid table-level governance and lifecycle coupling.
explanation:
Managed tables are the type to create, so that Unity Catalog manages both the metadata and the underlying data lifecycle. With a managed table Databricks controls the storage layout, applies optimisations such as predictive optimisation over time, and deletes the data files when the table is dropped according to its retention policy — which is every requirement the team listed.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (external tables with a LOCATION) — the customer controls the file layout, and dropping the table leaves the files behind; the opposite of the lifecycle coupling asked for.
Option C (foreign tables from an external catalog) — federated tables live in the source system; Databricks cannot optimise or clean up data it does not own.
Option D (temporary views over files) — session-scoped and ungoverned, with no storage management at all.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/managed

question: A data engineer wants to ensure that duplicate records are removed from a dataset based on specific columns before writing to a Delta table. Which Spark DataFrame method removes duplicate rows?
optionA: removeDuplicates
optionB: dropDuplicates
optionC: uniqueRows
optionD: distinctBy
explanation:
dropDuplicates() is the DataFrame method, and it takes an optional list of columns so duplicates can be identified on a subset — which is what the question asks for. Called without arguments it considers every column, behaving like distinct().
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (removeDuplicates) — does not exist in the DataFrame API.
Option C (uniqueRows) — does not exist.
Option D (distinctBy) — does not exist either; the whole test here is that three plausible names are invented.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/pyspark/

question: Which SQL code snippet will correctly demonstrate a Data Definition Language (DDL) operation used to create a table?
optionA: CREATE TABLE employees ( id INT, name STRING );
optionB: DROP TABLE employees;
optionC: ALTER TABLE employees ADD COLUMN salary DECIMAL(10,2);
optionD: INSERT INTO employees (id, name) VALUES (1 'Alice');
explanation:
CREATE TABLE employees ( id INT, name STRING ); is the DDL operation that creates a table. DDL statements define database objects and their schema, and CREATE TABLE is the one that brings a table into existence.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option B (DROP TABLE) — also DDL, but it removes a table rather than creating one, which is what the question specifies.
Option C (ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN) — DDL too, but it modifies an existing table's structure.
Option D (INSERT INTO ... VALUES) — a different category entirely: DML, operating on rows rather than structure, and as printed it is also malformed, missing the comma between 1 and 'Alice'.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-create-table-using

question: A data engineer needs to reduce the number of small files generated during streaming ingestion into Delta tables. Small files are causing performance issues during downstream queries. Which Delta Lake feature automatically compacts small files during writes?
optionA: VACUUM
optionB: CACHE
optionC: autoCompact
optionD: OPTIMIZE
explanation:
autoCompact is the feature that combines small files during writes. Enabled with delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact, auto compaction runs after a write commits and rewrites small files into larger ones automatically, which is what keeps streaming ingestion from accumulating thousands of tiny files.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (VACUUM) — removes unreferenced files rather than combining live ones.
Option B (CACHE) — affects memory, not file layout.
Option D (OPTIMIZE) — the close distractor: it performs the same compaction but has to be invoked explicitly as a separate maintenance command, whereas the question asks for automatic compaction during writes.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/tune-file-size

question: A data engineering team is using Kafka to capture event data and then ingest it into Databricks. The team wants to be able to see these historical events. Medallion architecture is already in place. The team wants to be mindful of costs. Where should this historical event data be stored?
optionA: Gold
optionB: Silver
optionC: Bronze
optionD: Raw layer
explanation:
Bronze is where the historical Kafka events belong. In the medallion architecture the Bronze layer stores raw ingested data as it arrived, which preserves the full event history at the lowest cost while Silver and Gold refine it for consumption.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (Gold) — the curated, aggregated layer for consumers; storing raw events there is expensive and defeats the architecture.
Option B (Silver) — cleaned and conformed data; raw history is not kept there.
Option D (Raw layer) — not one of the medallion layers; the raw landing zone is Bronze.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

question: A Databricks single-task workflow fails due to an error in a notebook. The data engineer fixes the mistake in the notebook. What should the data engineer do to rerun the workflow?
optionA: Repair the task
optionB: Repair the run
optionC: Restart the Cluster
optionD: Swap the cluster
explanation:
Repairing the run is what reruns the workflow after the fix. When a job run fails, Databricks lets you repair that run rather than start a fresh one: the repair re-executes the failed task with the updated notebook and reuses whatever succeeded, without recreating the workflow or touching the cluster configuration. Repair run is the documented UI label, initiated from the failed run.
Why the other options are wrong:
Option A (repair the task) — the object you repair in the UI is the run; a task is selected within the repair dialog, not repaired on its own. (A near-duplicate of this question elsewhere in the deck keys that wording, where the option set offers no better one.)
Option C (restart the cluster) — the failure came from the notebook code, not the compute; new compute runs the same fixed code no faster.
Option D (swap the cluster) — the same, with a reconfiguration step added.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/repair-job-failures
